member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank all the honourable members who have participated in this debate: more than 80 have intervened in this debate. i am pleased to see that members have acknowledged the importance of these three issues in enabling europe to drive the clean energy transition. i also reiterate that the three dossiers are strongly inter-linked and that parliament must remain coherent in its approach, and that the rules that we agree must be ambitious and workable in practice. on governance, i was surprised that some honourable members expressed the view that the governance initiative will undermine the member states’ right to choose their energy mix. the opposite is true. the basic rationale of the initiative is to fully respect the principle of subsidiarity and the balance between the european union and member states in the area of energy. this is reflected in the approach, which is through national plans set out at national level rather than plans being imposed at european union level. that is why the governance proposal is such an important proposal. some of you have also questioned, or raised doubts, on whether this proposal will be strong enough to ensure that the 2030 targets are met. my initial reaction is that the commission proposal was established in order to achieve those targets, but parliament has improved the proposal and these gains are to its credit. parliament has analysed the proposal, has considered the weaknesses it may have, and has reinforced it accordingly. i think that jointly, with the basic proposal of the commission and the improvements that parliament has introduced, we have a very important tool to make sure that the targets that we establish are achieved. because the overall majority has been in favour of more ambitious targets than those proposed by the commission we are at a very good starting position for the trilogues that are going to be extremely complex. without our good-governance proposal, all the rest is meaningless. today i want to thank the rapporteurs for their efforts. they have done excellent work. it is a very difficult exercise, and on wednesday we will have difficult votes, but lots of work is now behind us, and the commission wants to give thanks for all the effort made. coming back to renewables, let me say that overall the compromise text that is emerging in parliament also represents a very good negotiating position for parliament in view of the trilogues. mr blanco lópez has done excellent work, as has mr turmes and, certainly, ms rivasi. i see broad support for a high overall level of ambition for renewables deployment in europe, including the importance of europeanising renewables policy and strengthening investor certainty in this context. the regulatory framework that you are putting in place should enable greater cost-effectiveness and the sustained deployment of renewables in our electricity sector, in buildings and in the transport sector. on energy efficiency, i want to reiterate again the importance of maintaining a high level of ambition for article 7 to enable economically viable energy savings to be made over the next decade. how can we say that we want to do more to encourage energy efficiency if, at the same time, we undermine the best instrument we have, which is article 7. so there is a contradiction sometimes, and we have to solve that. i expect that wednesday’s vote will solve these contradictions. the debate on energy efficiency also showed strong support for a high level of ambition for energy efficiency and a strong article 7. that’s very positive. if you see what happened in the october 2014 council, when energy efficiency was proposed at a level of 27, the commission acknowledged that this was not enough and then proposed a binding level of 30. now you are proposing higher levels, and the trilogues will be complicated and the commission will act as honest broker to get the best final energy-efficiency proposal. there have been some more comments, particularly professor gierek, who consistently drew attention to the need for a life-cycle method to calculate energy use. i agree that this is relevant both for policy analysis and for policies like ecodesign that look at particular products. but if we apply it to the whole energy system it will cause problems such as double counting of energy use, so the commission prefers to keep the eurostat method for calculating energy efficiency. just a final comment to mr jávor. it is true that the media has said that there is a draft procedural report, but the final report is going to be released in october 2018. the final ipcc report is a very important input to the talanoa dialogue and for the preparations in the run-up to cop24 in katowice. but the commission will wait to see the final report to take the appropriate conclusions once the report is fully approved. i will just finalise by thanking all of the house for supporting these three pieces of legislation which are central to setting the new regulatory framework for the clean energy transition and for delivering our paris agreement commitments. this week’s votes will finalise parliament’s position on these issues and will be an important point of reference that will establish the pathways to a final agreement with the council. in the climate package with the emissions trading system, land use change and forestry we have been able to secure very complicated agreements. these future trilogues will be much more complicated, and i count on the good will of the rapporteurs and shadow rapporteurs, to try and agree the best possible compromise for the sake of european citizens for the fulfilment of our paris agreement commitment and in order to preserve our planet.

mr president, our constitutional committee has proposed that a quota of 27 seats be reserved for transnational lists. this innovation seems absurd to me, but it can make democratic progress in europe possible under three conditions. the first is to take advantage of this number to specify in the electoral law that each list must include one citizen from each member state, and only one. the second is that each european political family is committed to putting its top candidate (spitzenkandidat) at the head of its transnational list. thirdly, and lastly, that each government should undertake to propose as the first choice for commissioner from its own country the citizen or citizen on the list who will win the most votes at home. in essence, the transnational list would thus be the list of candidate commissioners and it would be the popular vote that would designate the composition of the executive body and not the governments in place. the governments which propose the transnational list swear to us that it is for the good of europe, but is their democratic commitment prepared to go that far?

the agenda calls for a debate on the commission statement on the summertime arrangements (2017/2968 ((rsp)).
member of the commission. – madam president, the request on today’s opportunity to debate on eu summer time arrangements is very timely. the commission regularly receives questions about the time switch, including from members of the european parliament. some of those doubt that we need to switch time. as the commission committed before this house, my services have reassessed all available evidence. this includes the very balanced and complete overview made by the european parliament’s research services. the evidence is conclusive only on one point – that letting member states free to apply uncoordinated time changes would be detrimental for the internal market. i am therefore against such a solution, whether that means simply repealing the directive or allowing individual member states to opt out of the harmonised regime. conversely, the findings are inconclusive on human health. some people seem to suffer from the twice-yearly changes, but this might be well compensated for by the positive health effects induced by increased leisure and outdoor activities. it is unclear whether permanent summer time or winter time would be better for the human biorhythm. while i am open to consider the summer time issues further, i would like to stress an important point. there are two options that would allow for a continued harmonised approach: stop time changes for all member states by amending the directive, or leave the summer time rules unchanged. if one were to select the first option, it would also have to be established when to abolish time changes – after the last change to winter time, or after the last change for summer time. we discussed the summer time issues at the last council sitting in december at the request of one member state. i explicitly invited all ministers to let me know if any of them were in favour of changing the status quo. apart from the one member state that put the question on the agenda, nobody has done so until now. today it is your turn. i very much look forward to the forthcoming debate and welcome the vote on the resolution which will give parliament the opportunity to voice its opinion in this matter. i am sure it will give rise to valuable elements for reflection. all the more so, since the success of any potential commission proposals intended to modify the current rules by definition depends on the stance taken by the co-legislators.
for the greens/efa group madam president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, in the transport sector, the twice-yearly change of time has a double impact. the first is that the lack of sleep it causes in many of our citizens is a real problem for road safety. it is the cause of a large number of accidents involving particularly vulnerable road users, and i am thinking of pedestrians and cyclists. a second important point is that the european freight transport sector, which is not at a standstill, has to cope with additional administrative burdens linked to the change in time each time summer or winter time is changed. add to this the fact that today, yes, it is a public health problem for humans, there are negative effects on animal welfare. i think we have enough reasons to vote in favour of this resolution by the committee on transport and tourism of the european parliament to call on the commission to take up this matter and to abolish the clock change which no longer has any place.

president-in-office of the council. – madam president, before concluding i will try to respond to your questions. there are many, but i will try to organise them and focus your attention on three groups of questions: those related to panama; those related to the criteria; and those related to the inclusion of eu member states in the eu list. concerning panama, i would like to say that, like all other jurisdictions in annex ii of the council conclusions unanimously taken on 5 december last year, panama made sufficient commitments at high political level to address the deficiencies identified by our experts, and this is a positive development. in any case, the delisting from annex i does not mean that panama is not monitored any more. it is simply not considered as non-cooperative any longer, but it continues to be under examination. at the end of this year, ministers will discuss the results of the monitoring exercise for all countries concerned. concerning the criteria, the criteria as well as the sanctions are available in the council conclusions from december last year. this is a public document, because we also put high emphasis on transparency, credibility and accountability. concerning the monitoring of eu member states, i have to say that the mandate for this exercise of the european union list was to look at third countries, because member states are already under permanent scrutiny as far as any harmful practices are concerned. every six months, a report is made to the ecofin council by the code of conduct group, and these reports cover both member states and third countries. they are also publicly available on the council’s website. to conclude, i would like to assure you that the council will regularly update the european union list of non-cooperative jurisdictions. this does not mean that it will be shorter in the future. jurisdictions that do not meet their commitment by the agreed deadline – the end of 2018 or 2019 – will be listed. the criteria and the geographical scope are likely to be subject to updates. the next ecofin council on 13 march will also return to this issue. work on further coordinated defensive measures will also continue in parallel. some are in the tax area and concern member states’ competences, but as you are aware, others are foreseen in various eu legislative initiatives.
member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members, first of all i wish to thank the rapporteur, mr erdős, for his report on the apiculture sector, which clearly highlights the important issues that have been outlined in relation to the bee sector and which can certainly influence the discussions in the framework of the future common agricultural policy (cap). the commission shares the view of the european parliament with regard to the importance of bees as pollinators for our environment and for agriculture, as well as the role that beekeeping could have in certain rural areas. it is precisely for this reason that the cap currently contributes 50% of the funding of our national apicultural programmes, which are drawn down by member states with a total eu budget of eur 36 million per year. the report suggests that this level of support should be increased. of course, everyone will want to increase their budget, but these are matters for discussion in the context of the multiannual financial framework (mff) and the cap reform. the commission is also developing an eu pollinators initiative to establish an integrated approach to tackle the decline of pollinators. the aim is to raise the political profile and increase the effectiveness of existing eu policies for pollinators. the main objective of the national apicultural programmes is to improve the conditions for the production and marketing of honey. given the importance of bees, not just as honey producers but also as pollinators, the commission supports them by other means as well. under the first pillar of the cap, 30% of the direct payments are linked to environment-friendly farming practices, while pillar ii supports agri-environment climate measures which also contribute to improving the environment for bees. while the report suggests stronger commission involvement in various research and education projects in the eu, we should also keep in mind the value of the national programmes, which are adapted to the needs of specific member states. nevertheless, the commission is closely involved in research activities in relation to apiculture, including the eu pilot project on breeding and selection program for research in the resistance against the varroa mite. this was recently initiated by parliament, and work was done by the joint research centre on methods for detection of honey adulteration. the commission also established, and continues to cofinance, an eu reference laboratory for bee health, and it frequently liaises with the european food safety authority for scientific advice on various areas such as pathogens or pesticides. the commission is well aware of the concerns about adulteration of honey, in response to which the directorate-general for health and food safety (dg sante) launched an eu-wide coordinated control plan on honey quality in 2015. the preliminary results indicate that adulteration, for example by adding sugar, is not only a problem with imported honey but also takes place within the european union itself. the commission is committed to ensuring that honey put on the market complies with eu standards and it is currently analysing how best to do this, although the commission is not convinced that new rules on origin labelling for honey could solve the problem. the cap also provides many possibilities for promoting honey. member states can include in their national apicultural programmes measures such as market monitoring or enhancement of product quality, with a view to exploiting the potential of products on the market. in addition, the sector is eligible for most promotion topics in the internal market and in third countries, and honey can be promoted under the eu quality scheme, either because of a specific link to a certain region or because it is produced in a specific traditional manner. the eu school fruit, vegetables and milk scheme that applies from 1 august 2017 gives member states the possibility of including honey in educational measures to be carried out in order to reconnect children with agriculture. the scheme aims to promote healthy eating habits and requires member states to ensure the appropriate involvement of their national authorities responsible for health and nutrition in drawing up the list of products to be provided to schoolchildren. several member states, namely france, italy, bulgaria, czech republic, greece, lithuania, austria, romania and slovenia, include honey in these educational measures. mr erdős’ report accurately reflects the importance of the beekeeping sector, and i have outlined some of the issues on which we can do more together. perhaps many people are not aware of these particular measures which can be exploited to even better potential by member states than they are now, through the apicultural programmes. i think it is clear that the sector is already well integrated into the cap through these measures and it also benefits from targeted, as well as general, measures. i acknowledge that the report suggests we can do more and provide additional support, so we welcome the constructive suggestions from parliament and i am sure they will provide food for thought, and honey, as the commission prepares its legislative proposals for the cap post-2020.
the committee on the environment, public health and food safety has adopted a report on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 76/769/eec on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the permissible sound power level of towed vehicles. madam president, commissioner, as rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety, i would like to sincerely thank the rapporteur, mr erdős, for his work, which is in the right direction in calling on the commission and the member states to ban neonicotinoids. the problem is that this ban is conditional not only on laboratory tests but also on field tests. the number of such cases is considered too small, which has the effect of delaying a necessary global ban. this debate is eerily similar to the one on glyphosate, for which we are promised a ban that is continually postponed. furthermore, the commission considers in its written reply of 1 september 2017 that neonicotinoids used in greenhouse crops are not dangerous for bees and therefore cannot be banned completely. these substances, even when used in greenhouses, are persistent in the soil and also in water. this is a real danger, since these neonicotinoids will not disappear for several years. in 2015, efsa confirmed that the use of this type of pesticide in the form of leaf spraying poses a risk to bees. today, a highly anticipated efsa report confirms the 'high' risk assessments for three neonicotinoids currently restricted for use in the european union. in order to avoid any misuse or illegal use of these substances and to halt the decline of bees, a general ban is therefore an absolute emergency. this is precisely the subject of my amendment which will be put to the vote tomorrow in plenary. it's about the future of humanity.

the rapporteur. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, since the last european elections, we are few in this house to have devoted ourselves to the fight against tax evasion. it must be admitted that this is not easy, because in four years we have seen many scandals, many revelations and we sometimes feel that our work, our proposals, everything we are trying to do with the commission does not allow us to move forward very quickly. and that is the truth, unfortunately. but that is also why, whenever we have small victories, we must draw from them a little courage, a little energy and, with this text, it is a small victory, a victory, albeit modest, but a victory nonetheless and we must act. a victory first over white collar crime, fraudsters, professional profit-leakage planners and those who obviously help them, i.e. the middlemen. there is - as you know, ladies and gentlemen - a real industry of tax optimisation, with discreet companies, and we ask them to be accountable for the arrangements they design, advise and market. with this so-called reform of the accis, all installations that do not meet even one possible criterion of aggressive tax optimisation will have to be reported to the tax authorities, under penalty of sanctions. it is also a victory over the unfair competition - the tax competition - which member states sometimes unfortunately engage in. all information collected will be automatically exchanged between the member states of the european union. any progress in this area is welcome, because we know that governments are engaged in a bitter race to the bottom in terms of taxation and only exchange useful information if they are forced to do so. well, they'll be forced to stay here, and that's a good thing. finally, it is a small victory for the european parliament, more specifically, because through the unanimous vote of the committee on economic affairs, which has substantially improved the text, we prove that our institution is one of the most advanced on the question of tax evasion. you will tell me that this is normal, since we are perhaps the institution that takes the sovereign, the people, public opinion most into account. on this subject, european society is tired of inequalities in taxation and is also rightly disgusted by all the scandals to which i have referred. people are watching closely what is happening in brussels on this issue and that is why we are and must always be in tune with popular expectations on this matter. finally, it is a technically solid victory, since the accis directive, as it is put to the vote today, is considerably enriched, and i thank, of course, all the fictitious rapporteurs and all the elected representatives who have taken part in this work. first of all, we have an obligation to notify the tax authorities of dubious tax arrangements, an obligation which will concern not only tax advisers but also auditors. for me, this is very important, because it includes the big firms that are systematically involved in tax scandals and are referred to as the "big four". you also have the profit leakage that sometimes continues through old installations that are still functional, and we have obtained, we ask, that all installations, even created several years ago, be notified as long as they are still in force. finally, and this is very important, we have expanded the indices of aggressive tax optimisation so that the radar is, if i may put it that way, as complete as possible. so we go ahead, we make proposals, we work with the commission. there is still a lot to do, but this is a small victory, a step in the right direction, which should be welcomed. i would like to thank once again the members who have dealt with this matter, and in particular the fictitious rapporteurs, and i would ask you to vote massively - if not unanimously - on this text, which is going in the right direction.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, although it is strange to have a debate in plenary without the council and the commission, let me congratulate the rapporteur, because he has brought some very significant advances to this legislative proposal, and all the repeated scandals we have seen show us how tax evasion too often involves the setting up of complex crossborder arrangements. these exist only because intermediaries, the ones we are interested in today, whether lawyers, accountants, bankers, tax advisers or wealth managers, imagine them and sell them to multinationals, those who can afford such a wide range of services. is it normal that whistleblowers should face justice for exposing fraud, while those who conceive them would be protected? by requiring the competent national authorities to declare, under penalty of sanction, crossborder tax arrangements in place for their clients, the text discourages the implementation of such dubious mechanisms which reflect a desire to circumvent the law or to reduce the amount of taxes owed. national authorities will also have to exchange the information collected, thus facilitating cooperation between member states within a common european legislative framework. it is now up to them to take responsibility and we believe that this is an important step towards the implementation of real tax fairness in the european union. we are of course waiting for the member states to take the lead. member of the commission. – madam president, madam rapporteur, honourable members, on behalf of the commission i would like to thank you all at the european parliament for preparing this important report. when i say important, i mean mostly politically important, because it calls for further mobilisation in the battle against climate change and because it puts some national actors on the front line, of course alongside the member states. this is, indeed, where regions and cities should be when it comes to finding solutions for climate change mitigation and adaptation. they have proved to be ambitious, forward-looking and innovative, so we need all of them on board. this is why is the commission welcomes parliament’s call to national governments to further support climate and energy initiatives at local and national level. it mirrors the efforts made at european level to ensure that low carbon and climate-resilient targets are well embedded in all our policies. as a matter of fact, it seems these efforts have paid off. climate mainstreaming: the target of at least 20% of the eu budget has helped us to deliver on the paris agreement and on our climate and energy objectives. for instance, in the 2014-2020 programming period, close to 25% of the european structural and investment funds will be dedicated to climate-related actions such as energy efficiency, renewables and water retention measures. we take good note of your call for the next multiannual financial framework to be even more ambitious in achieving the objectives of the paris agreement. i can assure you, on behalf of the commission, that we will do our utmost to ensure that projects financed by the eu budget are in line with these objectives. there will be no place for ‘business as usual’. in the meantime, the commission will continue to support cities and regions through the several ongoing initiatives. i have in mind, for example, the eu covenant of mayors, which has been contributing to our climate and energy objectives since 2008. indeed, eu covenant cities have already reduced their emissions by 23% and have pledged to reach –27% by the year 2020. i also have in mind the urban agenda for the european union, which was mentioned here by ms spyraki and other honourable members of the european parliament. as you may know, twelve partnerships have been put in place under the urban agenda, including on climate adaptation and energy transition. here, cities, regions, member states and the european institutions are currently working together on action plans to improve legislation, increase knowledge and use european funds more effectively in this area. i had the pleasure, for instance, ms ward, to meet the mayor of manchester last week, and i was very impressed by his pro-european approach and by his active enthusiastic work, hand-in-hand, alongside other cities. congratulations to all the cities. i think it is very important. he was present at another initiative we had last week on regions in transition, and manchester was selected as one of these industrial transitions. to conclude, i would like to mention that this year is the year of so-called talanoa dialogue. this word is from fiji, describing an inclusive and open exchange, and, in preparation for the next un climate conference (cop24), which will take place in poland in december, local and regional authorities have this opportunity to share their successful policies and good practices through this talanoa dialogue. i encourage all stakeholders to use this platform, and i think it will be a valuable contribution to our collective work. thank you to ms vallina for this report and thank you for your views and for your attention.

the agenda calls for the joint debate on:- the report by alain lamassoure, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a council directive on a common consolidated corporate tax base (ccctb) (com ((2016) 0683 - c8-0471/2016 - 2016/0336 ((cns)) (a8-0051/2018), and- the report by paul tang, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a council directive on a common corporate tax base (com ((2016) 0685 - c8-0472/2016 - 2016/0337 ((cns)) (a8-0050/2018).
the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, the accis project has two major political objectives. for companies, it offers a single tax space for the most important tax. that means simplicity, fairness, a level playing field. for the member states, this is the only way to put a definitive end to the temptation of some to reinvent national laws that amount to stealing tax material from neighbouring countries. tax competition is legitimate. it is still necessary to apply to it the same rules and principles that we apply to all other areas within the single market: transparency, fairness, equity. unfortunately, the european parliament has no right to amend taxation. that is why the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal of mr paul tang and myself, wanted to focus on three major policy recommendations. first, the project needs its two legs: harmonization and consolidation. all the companies we have consulted are adamant that the common base alone would bring more complications without the advantage of the common tax area. secondly, if there is a common european regime, it must apply to all companies, regardless of sector, regardless of size. finally, thirdly, this project is an ideal opportunity to address the problem of taxation of digital activities and, in particular, the particular business model of service platforms. these platforms have been around for ten years now. it is time that tax law took account of their existence and their particularities. for example, google and facebook have tens of millions of subscribers in my country and pay no taxes. our european parliament will be the first political institution in the world to put concrete proposals on the table. we look forward to what the commission - commissioner - next week and the oecd will propose next. i would like to make a political clarification. another project to tax digital services and specialised media is currently under way, initiated in particular by france. another approach, which is intended to be simpler and faster, is a tax on sales or on some of the commercial revenues of digital companies. watch your step! this project, which is presented as having the flexibility and speed of a cat, will still have the gestation period of a pachyderme and will, at best, give birth to a mouse, bringing in a handful of billions of euros a year. moreover, as with any indirect tax, the real burden will be borne not by the taxable enterprise but by its customers, with a risk of double taxation. do not be deceived! the real tax revolution will not be a short-lived pocket recipe, but the harmonisation of all corporate taxation. our great predecessors dreamed of it, and we must achieve it.
for the greens/efa group madam president, commissioner, the solution to corporate tax avoidance has a name: the ccctb, the common consolidated corporate tax base. behind this obscure acronym is a tax revolution. no more transferring profits from one branch to another and from one country to another to avoid taxation! this reform adapts our taxation system to the realities of our time. finally, multinationals will be taxed as a single entity in europe and tax will be paid where they actually do business, including digital companies like google or amazon, which will be taxed according to where they offer their services, not just in the country where they have their headquarters. but tax evasion has its accomplices, the national governments, who have been blocking this reform for seven years now. i said, "that's enough". they should stop being hypocrites, pretending to be outraged at every new tax scandal. let's get to it! that is what the citizens are asking for. if our governments cannot agree on this essential reform, i call on the european commission to use the powers at its disposal by proposing that this text be passed by qualified majority rather than unanimous vote. the application of article 116 of the treaty is the responsibility of the court. let it use it to advance tax justice, as president juncker promised us. those who refuse to act against tax evasion are destroying europe!
on behalf of the enf group. madam president, commissioner, the fight against tax revenue leakage by multinational companies, particularly us multinational companies in the digital economy, is the national front's top priority. tax evasion, tax avoidance and tax fraud cost the french state nearly €100 billion in revenue a year. mr moscovici, without these revenue losses, france would have a budget surplus. the functioning of the european union is the direct cause of this destructive fiscal dumping. thanks to the active complicity of several member states, such as ireland or luxembourg, companies like apple are able to pay an effective tax on their profits in the european union, which is close to zero as a direct consequence of globalism. we support many aspects of the tang and lamassoure reports, especially the concept of digital permanent establishment. this solution solves the problem of the intangible aspect of the crossborder digital economy. we also support the formula for the allocation of the tax base presented in the lamassoure report. this formula would make it possible to redistribute the taxable base efficiently to the states where the economic activity is actually carried out. on the other hand, we are not in favour of removing the 750 million turnover threshold, which would affect too many companies and not just the large multinationals. we are opposed to the federalisation of these new tax revenues, which naturally belong to the states. for these last two reasons we shall vote against. but the national front supports the struggle of the big european states against the tax vampirisation operated by the american digital multinationals with the complicity of a few small states of the european union!
madam president, new technologies and the development of aggressive tax optimisation practices by large companies are rendering the system for calculating and collecting corporate tax obsolete and making it necessary to set up a common consolidated tax base in europe. our corporate tax systems were designed for an economy in which companies had a physical place in a local or national market, which does not take into account the development of the single market or the rise of the digital economy. the common sense principle that a company should pay its taxes where it makes its profits is being eroded. that is why we are pleased to see this project on the table today. it has come a long way, and it has been revived thanks to the erosion of corporate tax bases and the multiplication of scandals, whether it be the case of apple, which paid only 0.005% of tax on profits in a country where tax was already very low, at 12.5%, or the luxleaks scandal, which revealed how agreements between luxembourg and multinationals such as amazon significantly limited the possibility of taxation. but we are also pleased that, at the instigation of your rapporteur and our committee on economic and monetary affairs, we now have the definition of a digital permanent establishment. this is a big step forward for those who want to effectively tax digital. on the basis of this proposal for a tax... the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, i thank you for your replies and i thank all our colleagues who took part in this very interesting and very enriching debate, which suggests that tomorrow there will be a fairly clear majority in favour of the proposals adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs. i would like to appeal to the council, because the ball is now in its court and it is time for the council, at the appropriate level, that is to say at the political level of the ministers, to take up this matter. we know - we have seen other examples and, on this subject, an example a few years ago - that the council knows perfectly well how to get rid of texts which are in its way, without having to vote formally against them. the first way is to say, "there are other emergencies", and in 2011, that's right, we were in the middle of the eurozone crisis, there was a fire in the house, maybe it was not the time to worry about changing the furniture. another method is to let the file slip by postponing it from one meeting to another, and this is where the priority in time that could be given by the council to a limited solution of the taxation of digital by an indirect tax could be detrimental. finally, there is another method which consists in emptying the draft of its substance, and what we can learn from the work of the working group, which works under the authority of ecofin, is very worrying insofar as they have completed a first reading of the first draft directive, by simply deleting the essence of the provisions proposed by the european commission, emptying the original proposal of its meaning. i therefore call on the council, on the basis of the commission's proposals with the amendments suggested - i hope tomorrow - by the european parliament, to finally address this essential issue in order to achieve the progress that the european union needs.

for the gue/ngl group mr president, madam commissioner, in order to function, a company benefits from many public resources provided by the community: school and training, health and social protection services, public transport, roads and various infrastructures, and sometimes even european funds contribute to this. these companies therefore have a social, territorial and ecological responsibility towards society and their employees. but they are obviously more concerned with their rate of return than with the general interest. we must therefore define a binding framework for social responsibilities. csr cannot be a hollow and ineffective concept as i hear it referred to here. relocations or reductions of staff should be blocked whenever it is a question of increasing stock market profits. when it comes to technological or digital modernisation that increases productivity, the reduction of working time and the promotion of training should be encouraged. social responsibility is also a new sharing of value, i.e. better wages and respect for subcontracting companies. this should lead us to create a minimum wage. it is also paying its contributions to the common good, when a study has just shown that taxes for multinationals have fallen by 9% since 2008. yes, there is an urgent need to set up an effective framework, not a hollow one as we understand it here, in the interests of society as a whole.
in writing. the reform of europass is, of course, an improvement on the technical side, as europass applicants will now have access to a full range of services on a single platform, from the design of online cvs to self-assessment tools or job offers. it is also commendable to recognise the decisive role of the national agencies in the operation of europass and to provide a rigorous framework for the protection of personal data. however, it is regrettable that the commission believes that academic and professional mobility is the answer to the real difficulties encountered in terms of training and employment of young people, since unemployment among those under 25 years of age stabilised in 2018 at a very high level of 18,4%. vocational mobility is a decoy, as differences in training between member states remain considerable, making it impossible to achieve strict equivalence of qualifications and skills. in addition, europass risks increasing immigration from member states with high unemployment and lower incomes than the european average, leading to a brain drain that would accentuate existing imbalances.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, at a time when we are concerned about the escalation of the conflict between the united states and china and its possible repercussions on the agricultural sector, i have come to speak to you about a sector which represents one of the most important challenges for food security in the future. whether we consume them directly, such as peas and soy products, or as animal feed, plant protein is now at the heart of our diet. these crops have immense agronomic interests and play a central role in the transition to more sustainable production systems. therefore, every effort should be made to encourage european farmers to use them and to strengthen their competitiveness. the future of plant protein in europe raises another question: what development of our agriculture and what food model do we want for future generations? in the field of supply, the signing of the gatt and blair house agreements and the opening of markets have sealed the european union's dependence on third countries. as a result, we now import more than 75% of our plant protein supplies from argentina, the united states and brazil, and this deficit is growing. today, countries such as china are implementing supply strategies based on production contracts with latin american countries that lack transparency, and the european union is at serious risk of seeing its supplies and the stability of its markets seriously threatened. this dependence causes irreversible damage to biodiversity, such as deforestation, but also represents a considerable carbon footprint. it goes against the demand of european citizens, who are increasingly expressing concerns about gmos, since the majority of imported crops, particularly soybeans, are genetically modified. with the successive international agreements, the adjustment variable of which is inevitably agriculture, and in particular livestock, can we really afford to put our sector, which is also distinguished by its quality and traceability, at risk? i am concerned about the international situation today, but i also have confidence in all the european actors involved who can help us to change the situation, be they farmers and their organisations, food producers, scientists, administrations and elected representatives. together, let us put together a medium- and long-term strategy that europe is sorely lacking. the european union must be more ambitious and have a genuine strategic supply plan that mobilises agricultural, research, trade and neighbourhood policies. developing a european supply chain and limiting imports would reduce the pressure on latin american soils and forests. the fight against deforestation is at the heart of the paris climate agreement. but let us be clear: there will be no increase in production unless we first improve the competitiveness of these crops. today, growing protein crops is still much less profitable than traditional large-scale crops. why is it surprising that only 3% of arable land in the european union is devoted to protein? however, legumes have their advantages: they have the unique property of capturing atmospheric nitrogen, which allows farmers to use less fertiliser. by generating many co-products used in green chemistry and for the production of renewable energy, they fit perfectly into the circular economy. i hope that in the next cap, incentives for nitrogen fixing plants will not be provided solely under the ecological focus areas, but through a set of measures in the first and second pillars, such as crop rotation, crop associations and support for ecosystem services. we must not only value protein-rich crops but also forage and grassland, as these are the largest source of protein intake in europe. this requires a clear increase in research, greater use of innovation and better territorial structuring of the sectors. finally, i hope that some crops will have coupled aids which are a valuable tool and will enable farmers to turn more to legumes. food sovereignty and security, the fight against global warming, a better closure of the nitrogen cycle and the upgrading of our supply chains: as you will have understood, plant proteins are at the heart of all the issues we will tackle tomorrow for the future of our common agricultural policy. it is essential that the future cap gives them a prominent place in order to enhance the services provided by agriculture and farmers. i would like to conclude by thanking the fictitious rapporteurs and all their collaborators who have made it possible to complete this report.
madam president, first of all i would like to thank and congratulate my colleague jean-paul denanot and pay tribute to him for this excellent report. i think we have to stop lying to ourselves, we have to stop lying to ourselves. we are, in europe, dependent on vegetable protein, as has been said: we import more than 90% of vegetable protein, in particular soybeans, which are very largely genetically modified. our european cattle are fed gm soybeans. that is the reality and nobody says it, when gm crops are banned in europe. we have to get out of this hypocrisy. we must develop a european protein plan, as jean-paul denanot has suggested. we must not only value the high-protein non-gmo crops, soy in particular, but also all legumes with seeds and fodder and grassland because, in fact, 70% of the protein comes from these grasslands. i ask the european commission, as has been said, to integrate this protein plan into the cap for the period after 2020 and to take bold decisions to make protein a value in europe.
madam president, ladies and gentlemen, when i listened to my colleague denanot, whose work i commend, i felt as if i were in the same room seven years ago when we were debating the häusling report. the same words, the same terms, the same hopes, and yet the same result: europe remains a cruel importer of proteins. we still have a deficit of over 20 million tonnes to feed mainly our livestock. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the decisions proposed at the end of last year on ecologically important areas are now being translated into a reduction in protein areas. the proposed circular economy policies, even though vegetable oils are a by-product of the production of animal feed, will lead to a decrease in the use and valorisation of proteins. so we must all be consistent if we are to make any progress on this issue.
madam president, first of all, thank you, mr president, for this good report. i don't get to say this very often, so i'll say it in the introduction. i believe that our aid often creates new dependencies and that our borrowing often puts us in debt. it is time to get back to a dynamic where we are in wealth creation that actually allows us to get out of aid and does not create new dependencies. in the old days, the bible said that after 50 years, debts were canceled. i believe that no nation can be locked up in debt. you are also right when you attack the "vulture seals". indeed, it is too easy today, but it is a general concept: man works for the economy, the economy works for finance and finance itself is governed by the market. behind this, there is no more sovereignty, there is no more development, there is the lockdown in debt and in the governing finance. it is a new imperialism that is against development in africa and against development in our country. i do not know whether the imf will find the solutions, we differ a little on this point, but i think you are on the right track and your report is going in the right direction.
the rapporteur. madam president, cohesion policy is a european policy which is unfortunately not discussed enough, but which, as we know, is essential for our territories. it finances a wide range of projects, from sme financing to vocational training and cooperation between regions. above all, this policy embodies a europe that is both concrete and local, since these funds, as we know, are managed as closely as possible to the territories. the proposals for the next budgetary framework of the union are imminent, and it is clear that we are hearing a lot about the new european challenges of defence, security and the refugee crisis and the reception of refugees. it is of course entirely legitimate and necessary for the european union to adapt to these new challenges, but i would like to say that the objective of cohesion and support for the territories has not become obsolete overnight, quite the contrary. the report i have been given shows that europe needs to invest more than ever in concrete achievements to get closer to its citizens and contribute to improving their daily lives. so, of course, we're not wrong. it would be wrong to claim that cohesion policy is entirely satisfactory today, but to guarantee its future it is not a matter of defending the status quo but of reinventing, redesigning and adapting it. the first project is, i believe, about simplification. with almost 800 pages, 450 articles and 89 annexes, this policy has, as we know, become illegible. worse, it is so complex that it sometimes turns absurd and discourages more and more beneficiaries from using it. however, there are practical solutions to make this policy simpler, more readable and more effective. this is also clear from a consultation i wanted to launch with the beneficiaries of european funds in my region of the pays de la loire. this survey, which i sent to 150 structures that have benefited from these funds, gave very concrete feedback to illustrate this report and demonstrated a need for simplification but above all the real added value of european funds for project promoters. this survey, which was carried out in a region classified as one of the most developed, also confirms that concentrating cohesion policy exclusively on the poorest regions would in fact be a mistake. the report therefore emphasises that the european parliament cannot negotiate the coverage of all european regions. several recently published studies show that while europe's less developed regions have experienced significant growth in recent years, many territories are still fragile and remain so. these territories are in a way caught between, on the one hand, the large metropolises which concentrate development and wealth and, on the other hand, competition with regions which are less developed or less favoured. the real challenge will therefore - i believe - be to ensure that cohesion policy as a whole is better adapted to the challenges of today's regions. it will of course be necessary to strengthen the social dimension of cohesion policy, but also, no doubt, to take better account of the infra-regional disparities, because our regions, including the most developed, have pockets of difficulty and poverty within them, and they must be adequately supported, which is not necessarily the case today. it will also be necessary to protect a number of territories that are sometimes forgotten by globalisation, such as certain rural territories, and it will of course be necessary to offer differentiated responses according to the specificities of a number of territories, in particular the overseas territories. in a very simple way, this is a summary of the report which will be put to the vote tomorrow and which should, in a certain sense, embody the position of the european parliament on the future of european regional policy. there would, of course, be much to say on this subject. in any case, i would like to thank the fictitious rapporteurs of the other political groups who took part in the negotiations and in this work. i am counting on my colleagues tomorrow to support this report and to send a signal in favour of a strong europe at the service of the territories.
madam president, civil society is not opposed to political society. on the contrary, it must complement it for a living democracy. citizens have the right and even the duty to express their views on all matters which concern them. unfortunately, there are a number of deviations in political developments both within and outside europe. indeed, civil society must have the means to resist these deviations. we must therefore help all these non-governmental structures to preserve democracy in europe and, from this point of view, i of course fully support the initiative. i would like to take this opportunity to remind you of the role of both the committee of the regions and the economic and social council, which we must continue to finance properly. finally, i would have liked to see the european parliamentary intergroups receive specific funding because they are a forum for debate between parliamentarians and civil society.

member of the commission. – madam president, first, let me start by pointing out that all of the participating member states have transposed the directive on the european protection order. the commission will issue the report on the application of the directive on the epo later this year. however, only today, the data already made available by the member states also confirms that only a handful of european protection orders have been issued so far, as was rightly stated by the rapporteurs. we share your view that we have to improve awareness among practitioners about this instrument. this is why we are actively promoting the epo. in particular, for now, we have collected practical information about national authorities competent to issue and recognise a european protection order. this is published on the websites of the european judicial networks in criminal matters and in civil matters. we have prepared an electronic version of the certificate on european protection orders in civil matters. this is quite a useful tool for judges. it is published on the e-justice portal. we have also funded training materials on the epo for judges. this information will soon be available on a dedicated training platform, also on the e-justice portal. the commission continues to fund activities under the justice, judicial training, and rights, equality and citizenship programmes which can include awareness-raising campaigns on european protection orders. we also continue to raise awareness with national experts from member states; most recently, on 29 january this year, at the high level experts meeting on victims’ rights. finally, the commission is carefully monitoring how member states have transposed the provisions of the victims’ rights directive requiring that victims must be informed about available protection, including in cross—border cases, from the first—contact authorities.

on behalf of the enf group. madam president, commissioner, this report reports on the implementation by the member states of the european protection decision system. it consists of applying throughout the union, for a convicted offender, a measure of removal, a ban on going to certain places or a ban on approaching his victim within a certain distance. on paper, this could be a very good thing, as the system should effectively protect a victim from further abuse. however, implementation becomes complicated or impossible because of the reality of a european union of 28. implementation is complicated, because it is necessary to change the law of several member states, without infringing the principle of subsidiarity and without doing so with sanctions that are and would be counterproductive for the women we need to protect. implementation is impossible, because controlling the movements of an aggressor in a borderless area as vast as schengen would require considerable resources and perfect cooperation between the police and legal services of the member states. how can you claim to protect women, children, the most vulnerable, when a terrorist is able to cross three states after committing a deadly attack? how do you want to protect a woman who is a victim of violence when entire neighborhoods of our cities are becoming no-go zones for women? the protection system that already exists in the member states is a good thing, but the limits you have imposed on it in a europe without frontiers make it ineffective. if we can find pragmatism and common sense, then the cause of women and their protection could become one of the priorities of cooperation between european nations.

the rapporteur. madam commissioner, madam president, as rapporteur on the protection of the european union's financial interests for 2016, my first objective is to ensure that public money from taxpayers is used properly within the european union. the proper management of public expenditure and the protection of the union's financial interests must be our priority. the results for 2016 in terms of protection of financial interests and the fight against fraud are generally positive. the adoption of the directive on the protection of financial interests and the forthcoming creation of a european public prosecutor's office are two successes that deserve to be highlighted. these advances will help us better protect the money and interests of european taxpayers and facilitate the recovery of eu funds used fraudulently. however, i regret that not all member states were willing to participate in the establishment of this european public prosecutor's office (20 out of 28 member states). in terms of the actual results, i would like to welcome the 15% reduction in fraudulent and non-fraudulent irregularities and the 8% decrease in their value compared to 2015. unfortunately, the very high number of irregularities still found in the fields of rural development, cohesion policy and fisheries is a matter of deep concern. i sincerely hope that the simplification of administrative rules announced will reduce the number of non-fraudulent irregularities, detect fraudulent cases and improve beneficiaries' access to eu funds. i would then like to return to some specific aspects of my report. firstly, i consider the undervaluation of customs duties on chinese products to be the major political issue in this report. as you know, between 2013 and 2016, chinese kilo, compared with the usual 26 euros per kilo. on 8 march 2018, the european commission opened an infringement procedure against the united kingdom in order to recover the €2 billion that would normally have benefited the eu budget. i would like to welcome the launch of this procedure, madam commissioner. in my view, the recovery of this shortfall must be discussed in the context of the brexit budget negotiations. the socialist and democratic group will be particularly attentive to this. secondly, i call on the european commission to submit as soon as possible a legislative proposal on the protection of whistleblowers, as requested by the european parliament's report of 24 october 2017 on this crucial issue. i also encourage the european commission and the member states to adopt measures to protect the confidentiality of information sources in order to prevent any discriminatory action or threats against whistleblowers. thirdly and lastly, i would like to return more fully to our fight against the illicit trade in tobacco products. as chairman of the european parliament's working party on tobacco industry interference, i would like to point out that 12% of the 6 000 billion cigarettes sold worldwide each year are the subject of illicit trade. the consequences are obviously health-related and as vice-chairman of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety i would like to stress that counterfeit or smuggled cigarettes are cheaper, more easily accessible to young people and more dangerous. the eradication of illicit trade in tobacco would reduce consumption by 2%. in the face of this challenge to combat this illicit trade, we must implement a comprehensive strategy to combat effectively this illicit trade in tobacco. these are the various observations or findings i wanted to make in my opening remarks on this report on the protection of the union's financial interests for 2016.

member of the commission. – madam president, honourable members of parliament, the importance of this agreement cannot be underestimated. the revision of the posting of workers directive goes to the heart of the internal market. the european project has been built around the internal market, which is the european union’s major achievement. but the internal market is not only about goods and services but also about europe’s work force. in order for the european project to be successful, the internal market has to be fair and also perceived as fair by our citizens. fairness means equal rules for workers when moving across borders and fair competition between companies. following the commitments made by president juncker to this house, we came in march 2016 with a proposal implementing the principle of equal pay for equal work at the same place. i would like today to pay tribute to the two co-rapporteurs, elisabeth morin-chartier and agnes jongerius. with their clear understanding of the challenges, their determination and their spirit of compromise, they made it possible to reach an agreement with the council on our proposal. also, thanks to the shadows and to the employment committee, its chair and staff. the text you adopt today is a substantive improvement of the rules set out in the 1996 directive, both for posted workers and for companies. posted workers will be guaranteed equal pay for equal work carried out at the same place. companies will benefit from a level playing field that will stop a race to the bottom on working conditions. the revised directive will tackle fraud and abuses. i will be very clear: this directive is indeed protecting workers’ rights, but it does so without introducing any discrimination of cross-border service providers. the directive ensures that undertakings provide services in another member state under the same conditions as imposed by that state on its own nationals. to dissipate all doubts, i tell you that this directive is not protectionist; its aim is to preserve fairness on the internal market, in order to preserve our citizens’ confidence in the internal market. that is why the importance of this directive should not be underestimated. we need it to prevent member states from having recourse to protectionist measures that would undermine our internal market and, finally, our welfare. this is the reason why in the council this text has gained support from a large majority of member states across europe, from east to west and from north to south. for the same reason, i count on this house to vote in favour of this directive with a large majority and to demonstrate to european citizens that the union’s legislative institutions can overcome political differences to effectively make decisions that matter to them.

the european union is a party to the schengen agreement, which is a treaty which is not a treaty of the european union. this phrase, which shows pride in progress, also sounds like a commonplace to which we have almost become accustomed. but we must be brave and firm to believe that this is still true and that this is still the strength of the european union in the world. but it all started so well when, in 1995, european citizens from 22 member states, iceland, liechtenstein, norway and switzerland were able to move freely from one country to another, which greatly improved social, cultural and economic exchanges. to ensure this, our predecessors established a common rule, which was ultimately quite simple in its formulation: harmonized controls at the external borders in return for freedom of movement within the space thus created. i'm talking about now, but a lot has changed in the last few years. it is because we do not resign ourselves to this slow deterioration that the european parliament affirms in this first annual report its commitment to the schengen area and free movement. it highlights shortcomings in the implementation of schengen policies and makes recommendations. the most important of these is shared by the vast majority of parliament. while several member states have reintroduced checks at their national borders, sometimes for more than two years, and although such checks are authorised by the rules of the schengen borders code, they are contrary to the spirit of free movement. they must therefore be limited in time and justified, for example, by security risks. however, while legislation to strengthen security at our external borders is piling up - member of the commission. – mr president, i would like to thank you for all the work that you have put into this file and for the continued support of parliament, especially mr marinescu and his colleagues from the committee on transport and tourism (tran), for the commission’s proposal. parliament has played a major role in these negotiations. now it is for plenary to confirm the compromise text that has been reached with council last december. this will contribute to our common strategic objective of achieving a deeper and fairer internal market while fostering innovation, with a strong positive impact on jobs and growth. a safe and competitive european aviation industry needs an effective and balanced legislation such as the one which you will vote on tomorrow. this new regulation is also a centrepiece of the commission’s 2015 aviation strategy for europe, ensuring safe, secure and environmentally-friendly aviation for eu citizens. it does so through a better use of resources, the enforcement of risk- and performance-based requirements, and by eliminating unnecessary administrative burdens. in practical terms, we are changing the certification process to be more tuned in for innovation, which means shortening time-to-market and keeping our industry more competitive. this regulation closes the existing gap in the regulatory system and introduces effective, cooperative safety management processes. importantly, it includes a system of pooling and sharing of resources between the member states and easa and establishes better governance for our aviation agency. allow me to underline other key benefits of the new regulation. it takes into account new technologies and market developments to ensure that they are efficiently integrated into the aviation system as well as subject to effective and proportionate oversights. this is in particular the case for the safe operation of drones, with new provisions regarding registration of drones and drones’ operations. i wish to thank again parliament, and particularly mr marinescu, for the strong support on this important topic. it is worth pointing out that we are going to get, for the first time eu-wide, a regulatory framework for drones. this regulation also takes into account the interdependencies between aviation safety and aviation security. in the future, easa will play a role in aviation security, including cybersecurity, and contribute upon request with its expertise to the implementation of rules in this area. another very important point for parliament was the establishment of an oversight support mechanism. this objective has been achieved. this new mechanism will represent an important instrument for a high and uniform aviation safety in europe. let me finally mention that the commission has prepared a declaration concerning the global navigation satellite system (gnss), as previously announced during the negotiations. the declaration should be attached to the plenary minutes and transmitted to the council. with your positive vote tomorrow, the new easa regulation could enter into force in the second half of this year. the commission is ready for this and has already started to prepare the implementation of this new regulation. commission statement(in writing) in the view of the commission, services consisting of the emission of signals by satellites of core constellations of global navigation satellite systems (gnss), such as the system established under the galileo programme and other similar systems, are as such not to be considered as air traffic management and air navigation services (atm/ans) as defined in article 3, read in conjunction with the corresponding recital, of new regulation of the european parliament and of the council on common rules in the field of civil aviation and establishing a european union aviation safety agency and repealing regulation (ec) no 216/2008 of the european parliament and of the council. this view is based, in particular, on the fact that those signals are not primarily or exclusively emitted for the purpose of air navigation, but are used for that purpose only through services that augment those signals, which are expressly covered by the definition of atm/ans.
for the greens/efa group mr president, thank you, madam commissioner, and thank you to our rapporteur, mr marinescu. sometimes it is not easy to reach agreements, but we have succeeded. i have to tell you that we have one of the best performing airspaces in the world in terms of safety in europe and it is thanks to easa, it is thanks to the european harmonisation of civil aviation standards that we have today this single european sky. but aviation is a sector that is changing and needs to adapt. on the one hand, technological changes, with the arrival of drones in large numbers. it is true that we - the greens - have called for the control of drones weighing as little as 250 grams, a european registration and a driving licence for all users. we've had fewer, but the most dangerous categories of drones at least seem to be well-regulated. we will, however, remain very vigilant about future delegated acts and feedback from the u-space programme led by sesar, to fully understand how drone air traffic can be managed in a way that is 100% safe and harmless. on the other hand, the airline is experiencing social changes. this sector is highly exposed to precarious employment in models such as low-cost or certain regular companies. we have long denounced certain practices that are permitted in europe, such as zero-hour contracts, pay-to-fly or the status of fake selfemployed. the legislation also links safety with the social conditions of airline workers so that a tragedy like that of germanwings can never happen again. finally, we are also seeing an acceleration in traffic: + 50% by 2030, x 3 by 2050, forecasts show an acceleration in the sector that is completely incompatible with the climate agreements and this is where easa has an added value, since it has environmental skills, so that progress can be made in the area of lightening materials, the use of hydrocarbons and the electrification of soils. that is why we will vote in favour of your report tomorrow, mr marinescu.
for the greens/efa group mr president, ladies and gentlemen, if we count on european roads, we find only 5% of all vehicles on the road being trucks. yet these trucks produce about 25% or a quarter of the greenhouse gas emissions from road transport in the european union. it is high time that we put an end to this imbalance if we are to meet the cop 21 commitments to save the climate and the planet, but also to give citizens a chance to breathe. monitoring of co2 emissions and fuel consumption of trucks is good news. until recently, co2 emissions and fuel consumption of heavy goods vehicles were neither reported nor monitored in an objective and comparable way in the european union. transport companies will now be able to choose the vehicles with the lowest consumption and emissions, which will reduce costs and pollution. we must not stop there, the road freight sector must do more and better to reduce its greenhouse gas emissions. the step we are taking today is obviously necessary, but it must above all serve as a basis for the near future, i.e. to establish mandatory co2 emission limits for all trucks in the european union. the commission has recently made proposals to this effect with a view to achieving a genuine and complete decarbonisation of the sector by 2050. i hope that we will be there, ladies and gentlemen, to give more strength, more substance and more ambition to this proposal so that the road freight sector emits 50% less greenhouse gases by 2030 and more by 2050. so if we stick to it, then we have a chance to meet our commitments, particularly cop 21, because we are all dancing on the same volcano in the face of climate change, so let's seize this opportunity.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, it was on the basis of the fact that 38 per cent of greenhouse gas emissions come from road transport that the commission presented in 2017 a system for monitoring and reporting data on co2 emissions from new heavy-duty vehicles. in doing so, the commission runs the risk of being incoherent. in parallel with this desire to reduce co2 emissions, which led france to promote the diesel engine, which allows it to have co2 emissions more than 10% lower than the european average, the commission has launched the hunt for diesel in favour of petrol. it is clear that petrol engines, which consume more fuel than diesel engines, ultimately emit 25% more co2 than diesel engines. so it's a vicious circle and the builders don't know what to do with it. on the one hand, the co2 hunt, on the other, the diesel hunt. once again, this will be a punitive ecology, with administrative fines that will go straight into the pockets of europe, which will hit the heavy industry to the detriment of a policy promoting good eco-conduct practices and supporting manufacturers and oems towards economically viable environmental objectives. this commission proposal is all the more unreasonable because it does not take into account the reality of the manufacturing and use of trucks. the manufacturers produce bare chassis which are then used for different types of transport depending on the box under the trailer chosen for the final use. the manufacturer's data thus becomes unusable and de facto useless factory data, but which will actually increase the final product bill. the only option for manufacturers is to switch to alternative fuels with lower co2 emissions, such as lng or electricity. this is already being done by many manufacturers; but the technocrats behind this text simply forget that these different types of fuel, while suitable for certain short journeys, are still and for some time to come relatively unusable on long journeys. in this context, it would be in the commission's interest to encourage the development of alternative fuel charging and distribution points before attacking manufacturers who simply meet the demand for a specific type of vehicle and correspond to current needs and possibilities.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the architecture of economic and monetary union has evolved considerably in recent years with the development of the banking union and the capital markets union, and with the establishment of the european stability mechanism, which played a major role in ensuring the stability of the euro area during the sovereign debt crisis by reassuring markets and providing financial assistance to various member states. because it is still vulnerable to the risks of economic and financial destabilisation, further progress in the construction of economic and monetary union should be made by transforming the european stability mechanism into a european monetary fund. this new stage should strengthen and improve the efficiency of the euro area in order to make it more resilient and to strengthen the protection of our savers. the fund will primarily be intended to continue the work of the european stability mechanism in crisis prevention and management. but it will have to be given new functions to encourage investment and to act as a safety net for the bank rescue fund. progress towards economic and monetary union will not be possible without democratic legitimacy, which is why the european parliament must be fully involved, as must the national parliaments.

in writing. on 12 june 2018, the european parliament voted on a motion for a resolution on cyber defence: a good initiative (in theory...) which is legally in line with the european union's strategic framework for cyber defence of 18 november 2014 and the resolution on the fight against cyber crime of 3 october 2017. we welcome the fact that brussels is taking seriously the threat of cyberattacks, the number of incidents of which is undeniable, and the threats both economic and terrorist. unfortunately, cyber defense is like a lock whose keys should not be given away. if each member state has its own system, it is all the more difficult to attack. on the other hand, the standardization or coordination of systems makes them vulnerable: it is enough to find a key to bring down the whole system. in the same vein, the continuous development of these techniques requires a high degree of reactivity, which is impossible to implement in 27 member states: we are witnessing this... moreover, as cyber defence incorporates military dimensions and cyberspace is increasingly considered as the 'fifth area of war', france must maintain its independence in this particularly sensitive sector.
