i'm the reporter. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, in my report on 3d printing i have taken up most of the concerns raised by my colleagues at our various meetings in the committee on legal affairs. 3d printing raises specific legal, ethical, health and safety issues. the issues are diverse and complex, but i have chosen to focus my report on two main areas: intellectual property law and civil liability issues, particularly in the case of the production of defective products. as regards civil liability in the event of defective or even dangerous products, the multiplicity of actors involved in the production chain could lead us to consider new provisions to cover and compensate consumers in the best possible way in the event of damage. safety issues are also paramount, particularly in the production of spare parts for the automotive, household appliances, aircraft and even firearms sectors. we have also dealt with the medical field, the production of prosthetic limbs and the reproduction of organs. this raises real ethical issues, such as equal access to health, and it is a health issue. i will also say a word about the economic and environmental benefits that 3d printing could bring in the future. i am thinking in particular of production and storage costs which will actually be reduced. the second text on which this report is based concerns intellectual property rights which can be undermined by 3d printing if the process is not properly managed. 3d printing may facilitate counterfeiting, not only by individuals who may benefit from the private copying exception, but also by organised networks making profits from the sale of counterfeit products. to this end, it seems to me essential to prevent counterfeiting that a legal 3d printing offer develops so that the individual who wishes to print a work can do so without breaking the law and ensuring fair remuneration for the author. finally, and briefly, there is a subject which has particularly interested me, and this is because of my former profession as an auctioneer, and that is the revolution that is coming in the field of graphic arts. tomorrow, everyone will have reproduction software or 3d printers that will allow them to reproduce the greatest masterpieces of painting and sculpture in a perfect way. the achievement of perfection in the field of reproduction is just a matter of time. so, unless we put a policeman behind each work, the question that arises is obviously that of the production of works of art, that of copyright and that of copyright. i ask myself: what will an original work mean in the future if the copy is exactly the same as the original? why is the original worth more than the copy? how can we protect ourselves from falsehoods? as you can see, colleagues, it is essential to be able to answer these questions by allowing greater traceability in the three-dimensional works produced. however, the point is not to curb innovation by law, by legislating more and more and by accumulating legislation, but rather to anticipate and see to what extent existing rules will have to be adapted or supplemented. in conclusion, we have worked on this report in a genuine spirit of collaboration with my colleagues from the various political groups in the legal affairs committee. i would also like to point out that it was voted unanimously. i the agenda calls for a debate on the commission statement on the participation of people with disabilities in european elections (2018/2647 ((rsp)).
on behalf of the enf group. madam president, people with disabilities have the right to political participation. this right is guaranteed by several legal instruments, including the un convention on the rights of persons with disabilities. this right to participate must therefore also be exercised in european elections. several measures need to be taken, including ensuring that polling stations are accessible, which is far from being effective at the moment. more generally, the public and the administrations must be made aware of the need to make every effort to guarantee genuine equality for the disabled in the electoral field. this equality implies that a disabled person must not only be able to vote but also to stand for election if he or she so wishes. i do not want to see a quota system, as tunisia has just done for the municipal elections. tunisia requires that each list of candidates include at least one disabled person. such a system may seem generous, but it is contrary to equality before the vote. it is also likely to hinder democracy by preventing candidates from standing in elections if they have not succeeded in persuading a disabled person to join them. everything must be done to ensure equality, but in strict respect of democracy.

convene as high representative of the european union. but let me focus now on four issues that have been and are central to our engagement. the first is the political transition. two-and-a-half million libyans have registered to vote, showing their desire to turn the page. tens of town hall meetings have been organized all around the country, in difficult conditions and with our support. the attacked in may, and since then we have increased our assistance. as i've said before, the libyans have to know exactly what they are voting for. a solid constitutional framework has to be agreed both the high council of state and the house of representatives during their visit in may. my second point concerns the security situation. the council is reviewing the mandates of both our civilian and our military operations and missions, working with the libyan authorities, the eu border assistance mission (eubam) and operation sofia. eubam plays an important role first of all in border management and we all know how crucial this issue is, first and foremost for the territorial borders of libya and for migration management but also for all sorts of trafficking and for counterterrorism reasons. however, eubam is also working on law enforcement and criminal justice: it has facilitated training for the judicial police and the criminal investigations department, and it works with libyan officials on border management. operation sofia is training the libyan coastguards and enforcing the un security council resolutions on the arms and oil embargo. so it is carrying out a responsibility and a duty that also comes from the un system. its strategic review is currently underway, and all the eu member states i discussed this with both the defence and the foreign ministers a couple of weeks ago in vienna have confirmed that they want to preserve operation sofia. its work is perceived by all the member states, and by our libyan counterparts, as essential for libya and for europe. so i cannot overemphasize how crucial it is that we confirm our commitment to libya's security with both eubam and operation sofia, working at sea and on land. the third issue is the economic situation. we discussed this at length with the foreign ministers in july, when we had libya on our agenda, and it is another essential aspect in helping to stabilize the country and meet the aspirations of the libyan people. together with the rest of the international community, we managed to contain the july oil crisis, but the underlying issues remain and could flare up again at any moment. the un security council will renew the mandate of the united nations support mission in libya (unsmil) on thursday this week, and the special representative has asked the mission to act on economic reforms: on wealth distribution and on uniting the financial institutions. this issue has been placed at the heart of the work by the un special representative, and rightly so. it is also an issue that the libyan authorities are identifying as a key element in handling and managing the current situation in libya, and i fully support this view. i think that handling the economic situation, particularly with economic reforms, wealth distribution and the uniting of the country's financial institutions, is going to be a key part of our work. so we fully support this agenda and, accordingly, we have joined the economic dialogue together with the usa, the international monetary fund and the world bank. our goal is to help libya implement reforms to ensure that the revenues deriving from oil can be distributed in a transparent manner and benefit the people of libya. my fourth and last point concerns migration. in our work with the african union and the united nations member of the commission. – madam president, let me start by expressing my thanks to our rapporteur mr corrao and his shadow rapporteurs, as well as the council, for this excellent outcome of the negotiations on our proposal for a directive on countering money laundering by criminal law. mr corrao, i do not see many of your colleagues here tonight in this chamber at this late hour, but as you see there are two commissioners present given the importance of this debate. today we are bringing all our member states up to international standards in the money laundering fight. money laundering, as you all know, is a serious affliction in our economies and in our societies. never far from the news, it is a practice which undermines trust in financial institutions and entire economies. dirty money is unfortunately also a key security concern because laundering is instrumental to the operations of criminal, and even terrorist, groups. terrorist organisations and organised crime need financing to maintain their criminal networks, to recruit and supply, and to commit terrorist acts themselves. money laundering allows criminal organisations to reap fruits from illegal activities and maintain operations. our existing criminal law framework against money laundering in the european union suffers from gaps and loopholes. all member states criminalise money laundering but the differences in how they do this, in the scope and sanctions for money laundering offences, affect in a negative way cross-border police and judicial cooperation. information exchange becomes difficult and criminals slip through the cracks left by divergent national systems. crime, of course, follows the path of least resistance and the criminals do their business where they see anti-money laundering measures to be weakest. the agreement you have reached in the trilogues will remedy these problems. our new rules will reinforce our capacity to tackle organised crime and terrorist financing more effectively by providing police and prosecutors with the tools to crack down on money laundering. first, they will provide minimum common rules on the definition of criminal offences and sanctions relating to money laundering, including profits from all offences defined in eu criminal law. second, they will also provide common provisions to improve investigations of money-laundering related offences. third, a comprehensive definition of money laundering, ranging from conversion and concealment to mere possession or use of criminal property and including self-laundering. fourth, liability and punishment for both natural and legal persons involved in money laundering, and fifth, maximum sanctions for those convicted of money laundering of at least four years imprisonment. this is the european union providing added value to the member states. my thanks once again to mr corrao and his shadow rapporteurs for the excellent work on this initiative.
the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the following areas: madam president, the fight against money laundering requires a comprehensive and coherent legal arsenal. the directive is therefore welcome because it harmonises the definitions and penalties for money laundering offences at european level. it also incorporates international obligations. this will facilitate judicial cooperation and strengthen our fight against financial crime. this is also the view of the european parliament's committee on economic affairs, which delivered its opinion on this proposal for a directive in november 2017, an opinion adopted without any vote against. as rapporteur, i am very pleased to see that many of our recommendations are included in the final text. it was important, for example, to add tax offences to the list of underlying offences in order to also punish money laundering and tax evasion. it was also useful to add the possibility of additional sanctions, such as the prohibition of access to public contracts for a convicted company. i would like to thank all my colleagues for this important work and i call on the member states to apply the european anti-money laundering rules rigorously and without delay.

on behalf of the enf group. madam president, commissioner, distributed ledgers and blockchain are promising technologies that could change the way we use ledgers and their data. however, your enthusiasm and the sudden enthusiasm of the european institutions give the impression of an irrational rush of new discoveries. so i would urge you to be more careful and more self-controlled. many parliamentarians only see the positive sides of this technology, without seeing its limitations, especially with regard to blockchains because the real revolution in the field of registries is indeed the use of blockchains. these allow the register to be certified and to avoid having to go through intermediaries to access it. however, this technology is not without its critics. thus, the use of proof of work in the mining process involves consuming a gigantic amount of resources for very little real utility. bitcoin mining alone consumes as much energy as austria, so imagine if you had to mine hundreds of other ledgers! the size of the registers is bound to become exponential and will require users, or 'miners', to have enormous technical resources to make the system work. this also raises the problem of the data retention time: can a blockchain retain data indefinitely without using a centralized archiving registry? the independence of miners is also a constraint because blockchains can only be certified if the majority of miners do not form a cartel. how can we control it? finally, the number of miners today is large and allows this technology to work, thanks to the payment of miners through cryptocurrencies. how will miners be paid for public services? many other examples could demonstrate that the technology of distributed ledgers, and especially of the blockchain, is still immature. until the problems of energy efficiency and an effective alternative to proof-of-work have been solved, it will be foolhardy to try to decline these technologies to all sections of society. what we are advocating is therefore to invest in research, as always and as proposed, and to let the member states legislate on their territory. let's give researchers and time the privilege of demonstrating that these technologies can revolutionize our world.

member of the commission. – mr president, it is a pleasure to be here today for the debate on the commission proposal setting co2 emissions standards for cars and vans for the period up to 2020. this is a key proposal to implement the 2030 climate and energy framework, to continue delivering on our commitments under the paris agreement and to contribute to the transition to a low carbon economy. this is not just essential for the climate, but also for europe’s economic prosperity and global competiveness. with the adoption of the legislative proposals on the 2030 climate and energy framework, thanks to the excellent work of all our institutions, the european union is turning its global commitments into reality and is determined to continue as a world leader in the fight against climate change. under the effort sharing regulation the member states now have binding emission reduction targets up to 2030 in the sectors not included in the european union emissions trading system – that is transport, buildings, agriculture and waste. now it is time to make sure that at european level we have the right regulatory framework in place to contribute to meeting these targets. with almost a quarter of the european union’s total greenhouse gas emissions coming from transport, this sector has a vital role to play in this transition. while europe has reduced its emissions by some 23% since 1990, road transport emissions have grown by about 20% and today, transport accounts for more than 20% of europe’s total emissions and this continues to grow. the commission’s legislative proposal setting the new co2 standards for cars and vans for post-2020 is therefore an essential instrument to address this. your vote tomorrow is instrumental to allow the adoption of the proposal during the current legislative term and we need to give a clear and stable regulatory signal to industry as soon as possible because this will stimulate the right investments in the transition towards zero emission mobility. i want to thank the rapporteur, ms dalli, for her hard work on this proposal, putting together the position of this parliament, as well as for our constructive discussions and cooperation. i would also like to thank the shadow rapporteurs for their work. i want to underline that the commission proposal, underpinned by a thorough impact assessment, is both ambitious and realistic. it strikes the right balance between the three main policy objectives that cannot be considered in isolation: firstly, achieving environmental benefits, secondly, bringing savings for consumers and finally, safeguarding employment and competitiveness in the european union. the commission proposal allows for a smooth, gradual and realistic transition to zero emission vehicles. the pace of the transition is essential, as the automotive sector is crucial for europe’s prosperity, providing jobs for 12 million people in manufacturing, sales, maintenance and transport and accounting for 4% of gross domestic product. we need to give sufficient time to achieve this reformation, to undertake the necessary investments and to reskill and upskill the workers in the current automotive supply chain. our target will have positive impacts on the overall economy. at the same time, the number of jobs will remain stable in the automotive sector. our proposal will also bring significant environmental benefits. the proposal is projected to reduce greenhouse gas emissions from road transport by around 22% between 2005 and 2030, contributing to our necessary efforts to implement the paris agreement. we have already agreed, or proposed, additional policies which will further reduce emissions from this sector, including the recently agreed renewable energy directive, as well as the proposal on co2 standards for heavy duty vehicles, the revised eurovignette and the clean vehicles and combined transport directives. from the side of consumers, the 30% target will bring significant economic benefits. consumers will save money – up to eur 400 for the average new car bought in 2025 and more than eur 1 400 in 2030. let me conclude by saying once again that the commission remains fully supportive of the efforts of parliament and the council to conclude positive discussions on this proposal still this year. i look forward to continuing to work with you on the proposal and bringing it to a positive successful conclusion. this is what our citizens, our consumers, our companies and our workers expect from all of us.

member of the commission. – mr president, honourable members, less than two weeks ago on 21 september, the commission published the vat gap study, which shows the difference between the expected vat revenue and the amount actually collected. eur 150 billion per year is lost every year at the level of the european union. we must recognise that member states have been improving vat collection throughout the european union, but such a loss for national budgets remains unacceptable, especially when eur 50 billion of this is lining the pockets of criminals and probably even terrorists. these figures show that the reform of the current european union vat system, combined with better cooperation at european union level, are needed so that member states can make full use of vat revenues in their budgets. in april 2016, the european commission presented a communication on an action plan on vat in which it set out the pathway to the creation of a single european union vat area. the commission announced that it would present a number of proposal for the fundamental reform of the eu vat system over the coming months with the objective of making the vat system simpler, more fraud-proof and more business friendly. this programme of reforms included the two proposals you will vote on tomorrow, namely the proposal adopted by the commission on 4 october 2017, which introduces the cornerstones of the future definitive vat system, together with four short—term improvements, or quick—fixes, to the current vat rules in relation to cross—border trade in goods, and a proposal granting more flexibility for member states to define reduced vat rates. considering the complexity of the past, the major subjects have been addressed step-by-step in 2016, but they all contribute to the same objective: to create a single vat area that provides for a level playing field for business; to create a single vat area that is fraud-proof; and to treat member states equally and grant them more freedom in setting vat rates. to start with the first objective, i would remind you that our current vat system is fragmented and complex to apply for the growing number of businesses operating across borders in the european union. such businesses have vat compliance costs 11% higher than businesses whose main activities are domestic. we have to open the borders of vat and create a real single vat area for european union companies. the proposals adopted in october 2017 presented the cornerstone for a new definitive vat system, based on the principle of taxation in the member state of destination, which will result in taxing cross-border sales or goods in the same way as domestic sales. these proposals also contain four so-called quick fixes, which have been requested by businesses, stakeholders and member states. the quick fixes aim to address specific problems encountered by business and tax authorities within the current vat system related to the lack of clear and simple rules, or even the absence of any rules at all. in this respect, the commission welcomes the support of the european parliament and the draft report on this proposal in relation to the quick fixes, but also the cornerstone of the definitive vat system and the concept of certified taxable persons. in may 2018, the commission complimented these proposals by adopting a proposal on the detailed technical provisions for implementing the definitive vat system. the commission also adopted, in january 2018, measures to simplify vat procedures for smes, which represent 99% of european union business. we also welcome the support of the parliament in this resolution, which was adopted on 11 september and we are confident that an agreement can be agreed soon in the council. we have no time to lose. we estimate that this proposal will result in a compliance cost reduction of up to 11% for smes. the second main objective of our vat reform is to address the unacceptable problem of vat cross-border fraud, which is estimated at around eu 50 billion per year. before an agreement is concluded on the european union definitive vat regime, i am happy to say that – with the support of this parliament – a first commission proposal to address vat fraud was already adopted in june 2018, only six months after its adoption by the commission. it will enhance cooperation between tax administrations and law enforcement authorities and close loopholes in information sharing. it is the proof that, when there is political will, things can change quickly. the last objective of the broad reform of the european union vat system is a full modernisation of the vat rates policy. the vat rates proposal is directly linked to the definitive vat system in which member states may be accorded greater freedom to apply reduced vat rates, because it will be based on taxation at destination. the vat rates proposal is also linked to the definitive vat system, because it provides a solution to the current unequal vat treatment of member states. it will resolve the issue of over 150 temporary reduced vat rates currently in place, which are due to expire with the entry into force of the definitive vat system, and which are currently only available to some of the member states. in a nutshell, we are suggesting applying the subsidiarity principle to give more flexibility to member states in a fair manner, in order to apply reduced rates in the sectors of their choice, according to their own national priorities. on the other hand, our proposal sets a frame aiming to prevent both excessive revenue losses for member states, and distortion of competition. furthermore, in the future, reduced rates must clearly be of benefit to citizens, because they are the final consumers paying the vat. where common rules lead to a better outcome, we work together with the member states. where common rules are unnecessary, and rule—making can be achieved better at member state level, the commission steps back. to conclude, let me say that behind the apparent complexity of some proposals, the reform of the european union vat system is a win-win situation for both member states, revenues and european businesses. more money to spend for public services, and more money to invest for businesses. with the support of parliament, the adoption of these proposals before the european elections will show citizens the added value of the european union and the benefits of a real single market for vat.
on behalf of the s&d group. mr president, commissioner, we are going to vote tomorrow on two important texts on vat, as a contribution to the establishment of this definitive vat system which europe has been waiting for so long since the time it has lived under the temporary system, into which a manifest fraud, known as the 'carrousel', has crept. despite the efforts of the member states, the vat gap - that is, the difference between the expected vat revenue and the amount actually collected by the member states - is €150 billion, of which €50 billion is due to the famous carousel fraud. reform of the present system is therefore essential. it must be combined with better coordination or cooperation between member states at european level to facilitate cross-border trade and, above all, to make the system more resistant to fraud so that vat revenue can actually be used by member states in their budgets. rather than taxing more on the purchasing power of european citizens, it is fraud that we must try to reduce. the system must be made more efficient and therefore simplified, and the socialists fully support the principle of destination, a principle which is endorsed by the reform proposed by the commission. but in the fight against fraud, we also believe that companies that play by the rules should not be penalized, and that is why we supported the report by my colleague, mr jeppe kofod - (the president interrupts the speaker) - and we regret that the council has not yet taken up the proposal in mr kofod's report for the status of certified auditors, which would allow them to benefit from simplified procedures.
on behalf of the alde group. mr president, i would like to thank the two rapporteurs for the work they have done in this consultation procedure. it is not trivial, we are united and our message to the finance ministers is extremely clear: this reform, which is guided by two key words, namely simplicity and efficiency, must be started without delay. the simplicity lies in choosing a floor at 15% and a ceiling at 25%. it is also a simplification which translates into a much more flexible procedure than unanimity for the definition of reduced rates. this is another simplification compared with what naturally remains to be created, i.e. a system of certified taxable persons, which will make it possible to access much less burdensome procedures and facilitate the payment of vat in cross-border transactions. the efficiency of the system lies in the availability of a comprehensive multilingual portal, which will enable businesses and citizens to understand the system. efficiency also requires a system of mechanisms for resolving conflicts between states. another step now remains, which will also be guided by efficiency and simplicity, namely the principle of taxation in the state of destination, one of the ways of combating the estimated €50 billion in fraud in this area. therefore, a single vat area for the whole union is in the interest of all - citizens, businesses and member states - except for fraudsters, which is also the aim.

i'm the reporter. madam president, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am very pleased to present to you this evening, finally, our final agreement, following the negotiations on the regulation on the mutual recognition of freezing and confiscation orders. it is true that the union already had minimum rules and rules on mutual recognition, but these were largely outdated. in particular, they allowed criminals and terrorists to exploit vulnerabilities very easily. that is why it was important to review the legislation and to work fairly quickly. the freezing and confiscation of the property and assets of criminals is also a tool in the fight against crime and terrorism, in particular because depriving terrorists of the proceeds of their illegal activities prevents them from carrying out attacks. however, in this area, we have a very wide margin for improvement, since, since we are working on this very important issue at the moment, 98.9% of the estimated criminal profits are not confiscated and remain in the hands of criminals. in other words, only 1% of the proceeds of crime are confiscated. this is unacceptable and cannot go on like this. european level and for europeans. i was pleased when the commission immediately proposed to work on a regulation, not a directive. even if some member states were a little slow in this respect, it is work of the bulgarian presidency and previous presidencies, the austrian presidency has continued to work with you to find a consensus to reform it, based on a balance of responsibility and solidarity. mandatory allocation, which is at the heart of parliament’s mandate, continues to be the main stumbling block in the negotiations in the council, and this divides not only the member states, but also the populations of the member states. we conducted bilateral talks with all member states in august, in order to find possible middle ground. this issue was also discussed at the council on 18 october. we are also working on the other files to find a solution to the whole package. this morning we were reminded of the tragedy of lampedusa. i want to underline that we have to ensure that no more lives are lost at sea. the objective remains to remove the incentive to undertake risky journeys by sea. i would also like to mention that in december 2016 the council adopted conclusions on the integration of third country nationals. on this occasion, member states recognised the important role of regional and local authorities, civil society and social partners, as well as local partners and communities in the integration process. member states were notably invited to focus their efforts on early integration measures in order to enable early access to education, vocational training and to the labour market. we all know that local and regional authorities play a key part in ensuring the reception of asylum seekers’ access to services and long—term integration into host communities. on the question of direct funding for cities and regions and granting them direct access to relevant funding, i can say the following. the multiannual financial framework provides long—term predictability for all policy areas covered by the union, including integration measures. the integration of third country nationals is explicitly mentioned in the amif regulation. local and regional authorities are eligible entities, the funds being channelled through the respective administrations of member states. in order to achieve the greatest added value, amif pursues strategies designed to promote the integration of third country nationals at national, local and/or regional level, where appropriate. in view of the next programing period 2021—2027, the long—term integration measures are proposed by the commission to be included in the european social fund+. this fund should focus on integration in the labour market, leaving early integration measures to the new asylum and migration fund (amf). the asylum and migration fund, which is part of the mff post-2020 package, should facilitate even more access to union funding. it should, as proposed by the commission, take into consideration the crucial role played by local and regional authorities and civil society organisations in the field of integration. in general, the amf should promote early integration measures for the social and economic inclusion of third country nationals preparing their active participation in, and their acceptance by, the receiving society, in particular with the involvement of local or regional authorities and civil society organisations. these actions should benefit from a higher cofinancing rate. long—term integration measures should be covered by the european social fund+ in the mff post 2020. thank you very much for raising theses important questions and for your attention. i would be happy if needed to complement these introductory elements at the close of the debate.

obligations under international law, the law of the sea, the geneva convention on refugees, the convention on human rights and the rule of law at every european level. europe must not be faced with the question: do you accept international law, do you accept the refugee convention, do you accept the law of the sea with limited significance? it must remain our legal basis. we should find a sustainable solution, not just for each individual case, for each individual ship. we in the commission are counting on the european council not only to discuss this but also to come up with smart solutions based on solidarity. the protection of external borders plays a role in this, and return arrangements in third countries play a role. but it is also a matter of sensible solidarity within the member states of the european union. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission is ready to provide any assistance it may need. when regions and local authorities ask what the european union and the european budget can do: the new asylum and migration fund for the next multiannual financial framework, which we presented in june, provides for much more resources, better access and less bureaucratic provisions for local and regional authorities. the sooner we adopt the next budgetary framework, the sooner the municipalities will have clarity about europe's financial partnership with the tasks of integration, accommodation and implementation of procedures at the local and regional level. the commission is also proposing more incentives for member states, for example by increasing the eu's contribution to the financing of integration measures. it is a planning authority which has been operating for seven years. we also want to work in the municipalities that are particularly affected - i can give you an example: samos, where we have a so-called hotspot - to improve the infrastructure - water, waste water, infrastructure in general - and where we can offer european funds so that the municipalities and cities that do more, which should also do more geographically, are relieved of the burden of what they have to do to organise a decent life for people who arrive in europe. we support the development of adequate emergency plans and have also provided funds for this in the european budget. the european support agency, which we are now developing, has produced a guide to emergency planning in the reception system and offers assistance to all regional partners. we are turning conferences into best practice, into city academies between practitioners and local politicians, and we want to help in this as much as we can as a commission. i would like to mention the european migration forum - a platform for civil society and local authorities - where we discuss and try to find solutions to migration management issues on the ground.in the context of the network of member state authorities working in the field of immigration, we have provided measures to strengthen cooperation between all levels and we have also provided funding in the budgets 2018, 2019 and 2020 that we can offer. we organise study visits for professionals: we call on the local authorities to come to the commission so that we can offer our network, our advice, our experience and also some modest financial resources. and it is clear that it is also about questions of legal immigration to europe, to the labour market. it's about reducing irregular migration through orderly gates. we have proposed a reform of the eu blue card to make the path to us more attractive for skilled migrants and to make it less bureaucratic, more flexible and easier to enter european labour markets. we need the social partners - employers, trade unions - to do this, and that is why we are organising joint platforms between the labour market players and the european union. in summary, the european union is of course playing a crucial role, but the integration and legal review is taking place on the ground. that is why the work of mayors and community social workers, integration experts, cannot be overestimated. it is our duty to support them financially, to build a network and to make their work easier. we can do a lot of things in the present budgetary framework and we could and can do this work much more flexibly than before, and also financially, with the next budgetary framework adopted at an early stage.

the rapporteur. madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, fictitious rapporteurs, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to thank the negotiating team of this parliament and the european commission for the work we have done together. we shall vote tomorrow on the report on the revision of the directive on the quality of drinking water in europe. the purpose of this directive is to review the quality parameters of drinking water and to propose a new method of risk assessment to prevent the dangers and risks of pollutants more in advance. almost 20 years after its entry into force, the drinking water directive is now in need of revision in order to align quality parameters with scientific progress and to take account of emerging substances. i believe that we in the committee on the environment, public health and food safety have adopted a coherent report which defends the interests of european citizens, which takes account of the strong constraints of suppliers, member states and local authorities, but which also strongly supports the european commission's risk-based approach. we all agree: access to quality water is a necessity for europe, a necessity for its citizens. promoting access to quality water for european citizens at an affordable cost, in full transparency vis-à-vis the european consumer, is also a requirement we can share. the report therefore presents several major issues: access to water, public accountability and finally the quality parameters required by the revised directive. on the issue of access to water, the provision of quality water is of course a priority that we share, but i regret that the european commission has integrated the issue of access to water into the revision of the drinking water directive, thus blurring the primary message on the quality of water distributed in europe. too many citizens still have unjustified doubts about the quality of tap water. it is true that our member states differ in their institutional functioning and in their physical reality, and we must take account of this diversity. the parliament's report already goes beyond the european commission's ambitions on access to water by proposing that member states promote universal access to water, i.e. access to water for all in the european union. i am pleased to have succeeded in integrating this balance, which respects the principle of subsidiarity and which i will be able to defend during the trilogue negotiations. the committee on the environment, public health and food safety called for greater transparency and public information on the quality of water supplied. the quality and price of water are factors which must be brought to the consumer's attention, both to preserve the resource and to encourage the consumption of tap water rather than bottled water. however, i would like to draw the attention of the european commission and the council to the fact that the objective of transparency must be to improve water quality and consumer education, and not to disclose information that is sensitive from an economic and strategic point of view, which in the current context poses a security risk. as regards quality parameters, i regret, ladies and gentlemen, that the world health organization, the leading institution in the field of pollutants and health protection, has not been given more weight in the original proposal and in the debates in the european parliament. in a particularly sensitive context in terms of health security, the challenge for the european institutions today is to assess the risks associated with each pollutant as best as possible. i find it surprising to say the least that the who, which is often taken as a reference by our institution to obtain more constraints, is now being bypassed by those who wish to amend the report in order to reduce the reference value for some of the dangerous substances, in particular chemical compounds such as endocrine disruptors and perfluorides. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, i think it is high time that a directive which is so important to our people should be revised after 20 years - yes, 20 years. my dear colleagues, ideals can bring us together, pragmatism and realism may divide us; i'm going to join the other side.

the rapporteur. mr president, i would like to thank each of those who have taken part in this debate and to offer some reflections. i do not know whether we represent one million, two million or 500 million of our fellow citizens, but what i am sure of is that the vast majority of european citizens are calling on us to provide access to water for all, which requires control of costs, control of expenditure, in order to enable everyone to consume as much water, and of good quality, as he wishes. many observations have been made on the chemical data. i wouldn't want us to get into some kind of a scallop race. science is science. however, there is no harmonised measurement standard for, for example, microplastics. the proposal before you introduces it. we know that endocrine disruptors have an influence in the environment. who tells us that it is not yet able to measure the exact health impact, which is why we have proposed the introduction of a follow-up until the knowledge is developed. i believe that the health of our citizens does not belong to one or the other. the health of our fellow citizens is our collective responsibility and it deserves neither over-bid nor discount. that's the meaning of our common struggle. water quality is one of the main elements of public health in europe. to have an excellent water quality for as many people as possible, and in the shortest possible time, for all, is to ensure good health for our citizens.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, since the 1950s, eight billion tonnes of plastic have been produced and less than 10% has been recycled. with time frames ranging from a century to a millennium to degrade, and exponential use in our societies, this plastic waste is everywhere, especially in our oceans and our atmosphere. france, the world's second largest maritime country, is particularly affected. recycling is necessary but not sufficient, since the production of recycled plastic requires the introduction of new plastic, contributing to the permanent increase in waste. similarly, some so-called 'biodegradable' plastics do not disappear. plastic breaks down into micro-particles or endocrine disruptors that are found absolutely everywhere. water, food, but also atmosphere, toys, floors, furniture, makeup, everything goes. in short, the dramatic consequences for health, and especially in the early stages of life, when our hormones play as important a role as genes in physiological development. here, the impacts may prove irreversible for our children. the only solution is to limit these plastic products wherever substitutes exist and then ban them from the market, and finally we must consider reducing consumption for others. france and europe must be at the forefront of this transition.

the rapporteur. - mr president, it is with satisfaction that i see this vast undertaking being completed today. four years, four years we have been working on this revision of the regulation on veterinary medicines with the triple objective of protecting animal health - and therefore human health - the fight against antibiotic resistance and the competitiveness of our farms and our veterinary medicines industry. we can say without blushing, the result is a great step forward for public health. i would like to thank my fellow fictitious rapporteurs, commissioner andriukaitis and the bulgarian presidency, who have all made it possible to achieve this excellent result. because beyond farmers or pet owners, the use of veterinary medicines affects us all. it has a direct impact on our environment and our diet, in short, on our health. the main focus of this review was the fight against antibiotic resistance, despite the alarming findings of the world health organisation. according to who, antibiotic-resistant infections could soon cause more deaths each year than cancer. the fight against this scourge must begin on farms where antibiotics have long been used purely for preventive purposes. in 2015, the use of antibiotics in veterinary medicine was still twice as high as in human medicine. the regulation should make it possible to change this situation permanently by means of more rigorous surveillance, a stronger framework for the use of antibiotics and the prohibition of the veterinary use of antimicrobials of critical importance for human medicine. it should also be remembered that the first of the solutions is prevention, in particular through biosecurity measures. antibiotics should be used only as a last resort and in no case to compensate for non-compliance with good farming practice. our agricultural model must adapt to this. i would like to stress that these new rules are not intended to stigmatise livestock farmers and farmers, whose difficulties we know, but on the contrary to help them to take better care of their herds, and because antibiotic resistance is a global phenomenon, we have been keen to impose reciprocity in our standards for the use of antibiotics in the text. it's a major success. there will be no more imports of meat from countries which continue to allow, for example, antibiotics as growth factors. no more hypocrisy in imposing standards on our farmers that others do not respect. europe is changing the rules of the game and they will now be the same for everyone. the text of course includes other important developments besides the question of antibiotics. through targeted incentives and reduction of administrative burden, it will in particular stimulate innovation in the veterinary market, which is facing a real problem of availability of treatments. it is therefore a comprehensive, cross-cutting approach that promises to transform the world of animal health for the better and in a sustainable way. these changes will benefit all those involved in the sector, which includes farmers and veterinarians, but also all our citizens who care about what they put on their plates. in particular, with its particular approach to health and environmental issues, europe is thus firmly at the forefront of the fight against antibiotic resistance.
on behalf of the enf group. mr president, this new regulation reaffirms the commitment of the member states and their citizens to the prudent use of antibiotics and veterinary medicines in livestock farming. the commission's proposals for a directive on the protection of the environment and the environment from harmful substances are not in line with the commission's proposals. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of animals used for scientific purposes. in order to protect the health of our fellow citizens, the european union must enforce its standards for the use of veterinary medicines and must clearly prohibit the import of products derived from animals raised in conditions which do not meet these rules. as with cloning and growth hormones, we must stand firm and not tolerate any failure in these devices. i would like to conclude by saying that in a very tense situation for our farmers, it is especially important to inform our fellow citizens about the care that is given to livestock in our european countries with very strict standards and protective of human health.

the presentation of this report today marks the culmination of a long cycle of work of almost two years on a fundamental text for the future of european transport policy. the revision of the european directive governing road charging systems on the more than 136 000 km of the trans-european road network represents a unique opportunity to take better account of the impact of road transport on our society. we are revising this text because the 'euro-redundancy' directive, which has made it possible to combat discrimination between residents and non-residents, has now reached its limits in terms of contributing fully to the objectives of the white paper on transport, namely to move towards full application of the 'user-payer' and 'polluter-payer' principles. without strong action and a long-term vision on the evolution of road transport pricing, which accounts for over 70% of transport emissions, we will not achieve our climate targets and we will not respond to the urgent need to better tackle the scourge of air pollution that is affecting our citizens. in the face of these emergencies, attitudes are changing and road users are becoming more aware and sensitive to the environmental impact of road transport. and it is in this perspective that we, as policy makers, will need to show the courage and will to accompany and accelerate this awareness and the transition to fairer and more environmentally friendly road pricing. and i take this opportunity to commend the commissioner for her political courage in putting an ambitious text on the table. the extension of the scope of application to all heavy and light vehicles, the progressive ban on vignette systems and the obligation to adjust tolls according to co2 emissions are all measures which i support and which are reflected in the report which will be put to the vote tomorrow. and the work in the parliamentary committee has improved the european commission's proposal. first, on the 'user pays' principle, the transport committee adopted my proposals to bring forward the end of the vignette to 2023 for heavy vehicles and 2026 for light vehicles, in order to accelerate the transition to fairer pricing based on distance travelled. on the 'polluter pays' principle, the transport committee voted in favour of the application of specific charges linked to pollution standards from 2021 for heavy vehicles and from 2026 for light vehicles. this proposal will make it possible to take environmental and social costs into account in road pricing and will ensure that around 50% of the trans-european road network is covered by the 'polluter pays' principle. alongside the application of these two main principles, the acceptability and transparency of toll systems are at the heart of this report. first, throughout this work i have placed a central importance on the territorial and social dimensions of road infrastructure pricing policies. and to combat the territorial divide, i propose to introduce the possibility of lowering the cost of tolls for frequent users, especially in the peripheries of agglomerations and in remote areas. the current directive did not provide for this possibility of differentiating the toll rates between frequent and occasional users. this is a major step forward that i am proposing to ensure that users who have no other choice but to use their car on a daily basis to get to work can benefit from a preferential rate compared to occasional users. on the subject of territorial cohesion, i also propose to give member states more flexibility to take account of the impact of tolls on peripheral regions. secondly, i am convinced that if we introduce a mandatory reduction in toll revenue to combat the deterioration of road networks and to promote the transition to sustainable mobility, we will strengthen the acceptability of tolls. the tragic incident of the morandi point collapse in genoa reminds us of the cruel lack of investment in the maintenance and safety of road infrastructure in europe. the proposals in my report which establish a compulsory toll will ensure that the revenue from tolls is put to good use in ensuring the safety of road infrastructure. in conclusion, i would like to stress the importance of approaching my report as a coherent whole. the proposals for the application of the 'polluter pays' and 'user pays' principles cannot be analysed without taking account of all the proposals aimed at enhancing the acceptability and transparency of tolls. finally, i would like to thank all the people and organisations with whom i have had constructive exchanges in the process of producing this balanced and ambitious report.

report by mrs lulling, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the proposal from the commission to the council (com (91) 0173 - c3-0314/91) for a directive amending directive 76/769/eec on the approximation of the laws of the member states relating to the permissible sound power level of towed vehicles many of the concerns raised in this debate are in fact already covered in the report, particularly on issues related to social issues and the principle of subsidiarity. however, i shall return to one particular point, namely that which would suggest that 'excluding light vehicles from the scope of this text would amount to 'defending' road users. it is the opposite, because to exclude light vehicles is to vote against the 75% reduction in tolls for zero-emission vehicles and to vote against the reduction in tolls for cars that emit less co2. the exclusion of light vehicles is therefore a penalty for users who will increasingly move towards clean vehicles and there should be no short-term vision of the future of road infrastructure pricing. excluding light vehicles also means voting against the reduction in tolls for frequent users who have to use toll roads to get to work. but that is not all, excluding cars from the scope also gives the possibility to states to introduce vignette systems which are more discriminatory between residents and non-residents. those who claim to defend road users by excluding light vehicles are doing the opposite: they are opposing fairer road pricing for taxpayers, who in many countries are now paying for road maintenance, and for road users who will not benefit from the modernisation of tolls proposed in this report. in conclusion, i would therefore like to call on all members not to lower the level of ambition of the text in order to arrive at a strong position of the european parliament, particularly with a view to negotiations with the member states.

economic development, gender equality. education, which is essential and demanding, is a complex and long-term policy, but it has been neglected. at global level, as at eu level, aid decreased between 2009 and 2015. it has risen from 11% of total eu aid to 7.5% and globally from 8.3% to 6.2%. this is completely contrary to the stated objectives. of course, efforts have been made since 2016 and they target of 15% of our development aid for education by 2030. specific objectives must be included in the next multiannual financial framework. at the same time, the commission must now consider how to the first is to ensure free, quality basic education for all. i am talking about basic education, which has been severely affected by the reduction in credits. basic and inclusive education corresponds to the twelve-year cycle of primary and secondary education and must be free of charge. so we need to support public education and not private commercial institutions that seek to profit from the education market, as they would from any other market. that's the first priority. secondly, we must increase our support for the least developed countries, not only because they are obviously the ones most in need, but also because it is there that aid is most effective. these two priorities are not the priorities we are pursuing today, so we must correct the course. the union and the member states must devote at least 50% of their aid to basic education by 2030 and at least 40% of their aid, also by 2030, to the least developed countries. so these are clear and specific objectives, assumed priorities. finally, this aid must be more effective, it is not enough to simply put in more money, it is not enough to simply respond to clear priorities, it must be implemented effectively. we need reliable, accurate and independent evaluation tools. member states' assistance must be combined, coordinated with delegations or joint programming. we also want our partners to take ownership of these policies and that is why we have chosen to prioritise budget support. finally, only one third of aid for education comes from multilateral organisations, compared with two thirds for health. the involvement of multilateral organisations, and in particular the global partnership for education, needs to be strengthened. we now have a clear and concise report, setting out policy priorities, the methods to be used and the quantified objectives. i hope that this text will be adopted by the largest majority in parliament tomorrow, so that it can be useful to all those involved in education.

madam president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i welcome this debate on virtual currencies and initial token offerings. in recent years, we have seen a significant growth in the use of virtual currencies and initial token offerings around the world, particularly in europe. these financial innovations offer opportunities in view of the speed and multiplicity of uses, but they also entail certain risks, in particular those of money laundering or fraud. the fifth anti-money laundering directive contains several provisions on virtual currencies, but this is not enough and nothing has been thought of for the tokens issued in the initial offers. it is therefore necessary to look at the whole world of crypto-assets, which includes, among others, tokens and virtual currencies. it is crucial that no legal loophole is left and that a framework is developed that can provide better security for investors and control tools in the hands of regulators. while classifying them as a financial instrument may seem an attractive option, all the implications should be considered, in particular the risk of applying rules that are not suited to this nascent sector. the europe that protects has a good opportunity to become a reality with its citizens. it is therefore important that the commission takes this into account and develops a european approach that is both protective and intelligent, while leaving room for innovation.
vice-president of the commission. – madam president, let me first come back to some of the points which have been raised during this debate. for example, mr rosati and some other colleagues were raising the point of cryptocurrencies actually not being currencies. that’s why, from the european commission side, we also change the terminology and we’re no longer talking about cryptocurrencies, we’re talking about cryptoassets. because, indeed, there is only one currency in the euro area and it’s the euro, so the rest is cryptoassets. second, on the need also for international cooperation in this area. cryptoassets and blockchains are a global phenomenon. as regards policy and regulation, to be effective it also needs to be internationally coordinated, so we need to do our homework here at eu level but also need to coordinate this work internationally. at the eu level, as i said, we need to complete our assessment of the applicability and suitability of existing rules and, together with european supervisory authorities, we intend to do so by the end of the year. based on this assessment, then we need to look at what is the best way forward for risks to be confined and monitored, consumers and investors to be protected and innovation to be encouraged. in addressing legal uncertainty and risks for market integrity, investor and consumer protection or security requirements, we should not throw the baby out with the bathwater. the underlying technologies which make cryptoassets work and spread have major potential across sectors. it is a new development, so we need to make an informed decision to find a right balance. so, once again, based on assessment of the applicability and suitability of existing rules and regulations, the commission will consider if measures are required at eu level to seize opportunities and address the risks.

member of the commission. – madam president, i welcome this opportunity to join you today to discuss the un global compact for safe, orderly and regular migration, in particular as we approach the final stage of the process – its adoption. in our globalised world, human mobility can only be addressed effectively by the international community as a whole. it is a global phenomenon that requires global solutions, a global response. no country can manage this alone, but together we can set up a humane, dignified and secure mechanism for governing human mobility. this is why the commission strongly supports the global compacts and will be actively engaging in their follow—up. over the past years, the european union has built a comprehensive approach to address migration and forced displacement. our approach has proved to be the right one and delivers results. all this was possible thanks to our common work inside the european union, and to strong cooperation with our partners, in our region and also worldwide. our approach is based on solidarity, shared responsibility, multilateralism and engagement. and this is exactly what the un global compact for migration is about, as the un compact on refugees. the migration compact is the result of two years of intensive consultations and negotiations at the un level, involving governments and other actors. it is the first ever agreement at international level on migration. the commitment to work together to improve cooperation on international migration in order to make it safe, orderly and regular. we all know that the text is not perfect. as you know, ‘perfect’ is the enemy of good! as in any international negotiations, eu member states had to make compromises with states from other regions in the world that have a different perspective on migration. but overall, we have good reasons to be satisfied with the global compact on migration. the final text of the gcm contains many actions that will help us firstly to improve the situation for migrants; secondly, to reduce irregular migration; thirdly, to address the drivers of migration, fight trafficking in human beings and migrant smuggling, and manage borders and facilitate return and readmission. several misconceptions on the compacts have been floating around. i think we need to address them. first, the compact is not legally binding. it will not create any legal obligations for states. it is a menu of policy actions and best practices from which states may draw to implement their national migration policies. more than that, it is fully in line with the principle of national sovereignty and fully respects the sovereign right of states to determine their national migration policies. second, the compact does not encourage migration, nor does it discourage it; what it aims at is that migration takes place in a safe and orderly manner. it contains no language to promote a ‘human right to migrate’, but it stresses the need to protect migrants’ human rights. migration has been part of the human experience throughout history. it is our task to make it work for all. the compact as an international cooperative framework will usefully underpin our existing work with third countries and international organisations such as iom and unhcr. it will also serve as a platform for new partnerships. europe is already at the forefront of migration and has a developed migration policy with high standards for migrants and refugees. the compacts will allow promoting the same standards outside the union borders, thus improving international cooperation on migration in all its aspects. it will help to jointly turn migration from a european and national challenge into a shared one, and into an opportunity for human development, in line with the 2030 agenda for sustainable development. we all supported the un initiative to hold a high-level meeting on migration at the 2016 united nations general assembly (unga). the unanimously adopted new york declaration launched the work on the two global compacts, on refugees and on migration. the eu took an early lead in the discussions on the global migration compact and participated actively in the preparatory work. our delegation in new york has been working closely with our member states in order to ensure that the european union’s priorities were reflected in the final text. we have done so together with the 27 member states that have been actively negotiating and speaking with one voice. this has allowed us to bring forward a global migration compact that largely reflects european objectives and respects our key concerns. we therefore regret the decision by some eu member states not to support the global compact on migration. it is their national decision, which does not affect the position of the commission. the commission will continue our work to improve migration management worldwide. this is what the eu acquis on migration and development leads to. we will notably continue our engagement with the iom, which will lead on the implementation of and follow-up to the compact, which will entail sharing experiences, helping countries to overcome shortcomings and searching for solutions to a global issue. we will also continue to support partnerships at bilateral, regional and global level in the area of migration. with our partners in the world, the migration compact will be an important basis for cooperation along with what has been agreed as the common eu approach to migration. here our common work and your contribution as the european parliament will be essential, dear colleagues.

member of the commission. – mr president, lyme disease, or borreliosis, is a real health concern for european citizens, who are increasingly exposed to ticks and the associated risks of lyme disease. in fact, lyme disease is the most prevalent tick-transmitted infection in europe. recent studies estimate that the incidence of lyme disease at 22 cases per 100 000 persons per year, with a steadily increasing occurrence in several member states. in the absence of a consistent surveillance system in the past, it remains difficult to accurately assess the overall trend of lyme disease. it is, however, clear that the northward spread of ticks and adaptation of altitude are associated with climate change and land-use change. currently, there is no vaccine against lyme disease so the recommendation is to take general prevention methods, such as tick awareness, appropriate clothing in tick-infested areas and the removal of attached ticks. these are particularly important for citizens living in areas where lyme disease is endemic and high-risk groups, such as agricultural and forestry workers. let me now address each of the questions you raised. question one: the european centre for disease prevention and control (ecdc) and member state experts worked on a proposal to include lyme disease on the eu list of notifiable diseases. however, the diagnosis of lyme disease is challenging, as the symptoms are varied and often non—specific. in addition, different diagnostic criteria and tests are used in different countries. thus, the disease may go undetected, with the subsequent risk of developing serious chronic manifestations. neuroborreliosis is the most serious complication of the borrelia bacterial infection, seen in about 10% of patients with lyme disease. the definition of neuroborreliosis is more standardised than other lyme disease manifestations, with the possibility to confirm cases based on a common eu case definition. this is why, based on a scientific assessment, it was therefore decided to include lyme neuroborreliosis in the list of eu notifiable diseases under the decision on serious cross—border threats to health. the commission remains fully committed to tackle the disease, working with member states to strengthen prevention, surveillance and control of lyme disease. as a key element, the decision on serious cross—border threats to health, which i have just mentioned, provides for epidemiological surveillance of communicable diseases through the use of comparable and compatible data. question two: with the recent inclusion of lyme neuroborreliosis in the list of eu notifiable diseases, all eu and eea member states are required to report such cases using the standard eu case definition. the epidemiological information on neuroborreliosis will be collected by the european centre for disease prevention and control, starting in 2019 for cases diagnosed in 2018. in time, this will allow a better evaluation of the disease prevalence and trend of lyme disease in europe. cooperation on surveillance, prevention and control between member states is ongoing, coordinated by the centre. question three: the centre is actively contributing to enhance awareness about lyme disease among professionals and the general population. several publications and tools are available, including information about the disease and the vector infographics disease fact-sheets for professionals and health practitioners and a communication toolkit on tick-borne diseases and preventive measures against tick bites. to strengthen preparedness and exchange of best practices, the commission organised a workshop on the challenges of managing outbreaks of vector-borne diseases in september 2017. the centre has also conducted community preparedness case studies, including on lyme disease, focusing on synergies on community and hospitals. question four: as regards diagnostic practices, reporting of lyme neuroborreliosis cases from 2018 onwards will be done according to a common case definition and diagnostic criteria. this will help to allow for a more accurate picture of the prevalence of lyme disease in the eu. in addition, the european centre for disease prevention and control has conducted a systematic literature review on the diagnostic accuracy of serological tests for lyme disease. it will start collecting data on the laboratory methods to evaluate the diagnosis for lyme neuroborreliosis in 2019. question five: as you know, the commission is not in a position to harmonise treatment practices as this falls within the competence of the member states. this being said, the commission is committed to help develop new and better diagnostics for lyme disease. this effort has seen significant financial support in recent years. question six: let me highlight that there is indeed currently very significant funding behind efforts to improve the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of lyme disease in the eu. the commission has recently supported research on improved diagnostics that will permit early and accurate diagnosis of lyme disease through the provision of eur 7.8 million. it is also worth noting that, in 2016, the european investment bank granted eur 25 million for the development of a lyme vaccine. additionally, the commission has provided eur 3 million to fund the development of an anti-tick vaccine aiming to protect against all tick-borne diseases in europe. the remaining two years of horizon 2020, and in particular its forthcoming calls for research and innovation project proposals, will offer further opportunities to support research on lyme disease. we now need to implement a robust lyme disease surveillance to have a clearer picture on the disease burden and trends across the eu. we will further focus on awareness raising, improving community preparedness and prevention and supporting research efforts to develop new diagnostic methods and vaccines. i hope, and indeed trust, you share the intention to drive matters forward, to strengthen prevention and reduce the prevalence and the suffering associated with lyme disease.

for the gue/ngl group mr president, there are some subjects which are difficult to debate because they quickly unleash passion, which often prevents reason from coming first. we have, however, largely escaped this in the context of these special committees, and i welcome this, even though our views may differ quite widely. we agree on one thing. our citizens have a right to security, and the fight against terrorism must be a priority. but our citizens also have a right to security, which means that their rights must be protected, including against the risks of abuse of power by public authorities. this means that the end, however legitimate, does not justify any means and, in particular, that any infringement of rights and freedoms must be justified by the principles of necessity, finality and proportionality. that is why we are against the increase in the exchange of information. an increasing number of people are being arrested, including those who may have been intending to commit an act. this theory of generalized suspicion is not the right method, especially of prevention. there is no justification for a hierarchy of fundamental rights, just as there can be no second-class citizens or second-generation citizens with different rights. we reject the stigmatisation of whole sections of the population. although improved during the negotiations, this report still falls short of our expectations. it proposes to pursue what i would call, for lack of time, a security leap forward, particularly in the area of border controls, and it does not avoid certain amalgamations with migration issues. democracy is the balance between safety, security and the protection of fundamental rights. to abandon it is to give the floor to what we are supposed to be fighting against, which is why we will not vote for this report.
