vice-president of the commission / high representative of the union for foreign affairs and security policy. – madam president, the fate of selahattin demirtaş is an issue which, i believe, lies close to the hearts of many of us. he has been for long years an interlocutor for many and a key figure in turkey’s democratic debate. so today we are discussing not just the fate of a human being, which is probably the most important thing the chamber can discuss, but also the state of turkey’s democracy. we are discussing the individual and collective rights of all turkish citizens. in the past two years, we have witnessed the detention of elected politicians, journalists and academics. we are well aware of the incredible challenge that turkey faced, back in july 2016, with the attempted coup d’état but today the state of emergency is over and this should be the time to strengthen turkey’s democracy. the independence of turkey’s judiciary is being undermined. fundamental rights such as the presumption of innocence are often ignored and violated. on the one hand, the case of mr demirtaş reflects these wider trends and, on the other hand, this case is quite unique. demirtaş is a member of parliament, a former presidential candidate, the co-chair of his party and a democratically elected leader. his case is about pluralism in turkey and the right of every individual freely to take part in their country’s democratic life, and, for this reason too, we have followed his case since his detention more than two years ago. on the day of his detention, commissioner hahn and i described him as ‘our trusted and valued interlocutor’, and i believe many in this chamber will share these views. as you know, i raised this case again, in public and in private, during my last meeting with foreign minister mevlüt çavuşoğlu at the high level political dialogue in ankara last month. that, by the way, was a very fruitful, open and constructive meeting, and i’m very happy about that. this was just two days after the ruling by the european court of human rights which we are discussing today. the court had ruled that mr demirtaş’ extended detention violated the european convention on human rights. as commissioner hahn and i said in ankara, just a couple of weeks ago during this meeting, we expect the turkish authorities, including the turkish judiciary, to follow up in an appropriate manner on the recommendations by the council of europe and on the rulings by the european court of human rights. we expect to see concrete progress in turkey on the rule of law and fundamental freedoms, including those of mr demirtaş. the court in this case has described his detention as an unjustified interference with the free expression of the turkish people’s opinion and with his right to be elected and to sit in parliament. the court found, ‘beyond reasonable doubt’ that his time in prison had the purpose to suffocate pluralism and turkey’s democratic debate. let me remind everyone that the european convention on human rights does not belong to the european union nor to any of our member states. it is the result of work done in the 1950s by the council of europe, and turkey is a proud founding member of the council of europe. the european convention on human rights is embedded in turkey’s domestic law so this is a violation not of a recommendation from the european union but of turkey’s own laws, principles and values. mr demirtaş’ legal status has changed now, following a recent ruling in another case by a turkish court of appeal. nonetheless, i believe that it is not only turkey’s responsibility but also in turkey’s interest to follow up immediately on rulings by the european court of human rights. this is not just about turkey’s status as a candidate country. i would like to be very clear on this. i believe it is about the kind of country the turkish people and citizens want and deserve: a country with stronger institutions, a more inclusive country, and a country where all the people of turkey can find their place and contribute to turkish society’s collective progress. what we would like to see, as the european union, is a strong, free, secure, prosperous and democratic turkey as a key neighbour and partner in our region, not just as a candidate country. it is in our shared interest to contribute to this, and all the turkish people should know that they can count on the european union to be at their side for a secure, democratic, free and prosperous turkey.

mr president, the added value of the european union is not always visible to our citizens. however, there is one achievement of this mandate that we can look forward to: the creation of a european public prosecutor's office to protect the financial interests of the union. unfortunately, we'll have to wait until 2020 to see it work. i say unfortunately because the conclusions of the commission's legal services on the conflict of interest of the czech prime minister could have been followed by an independent investigation by the european public prosecutor's office, in order to find out precisely how the subsidies in question were allocated and spent. by diverting european funds from their primary purpose, mr babiš is not only depriving his country of essential funding, he is playing a game with all european citizens. pending the implementation of the european public prosecutor's office, it is therefore up to the czech authorities to conduct an independent investigation, this is the only way to recover this money and the trust of the citizens. it is a question of credibility, it is also a question of democracy.
mr president, the severity of the balkan winter cannot hide a reality which is now so undeniable that even the coordinator of the international organisation for migration in sarajevo reluctantly admitted it, namely that 85% of the pseudo-refugees stationed in bosnia-herzegovina are in fact economic migrants, demonstrating that, in the face of this flood of migration, denial is no longer even a recipe. the new balkan route is largely successful: three quarters of migrants passing through bosnia and herzegovina would be able to leave, free to wander as they wish in europe. the vast majority of them will never be deported. whose fault is it? the european union, of course. we are happy to pour millions into the danaid barrel of the migrant crisis, when in reality the only people we should be supporting are the croatian security forces and the serbs of bosnia and herzegovina, represented by milorad dodik, who are fighting bravely against a real overwhelm to which all seem to have now capitulated.

on behalf of the enf group. mr president, no less than seven rapporteurs have just spoken out against egypt, and yet marshal al-sissi is a bulwark against islamism. he came to power in 2013 by overthrowing islamist president mohamed morsi, who was on the verge of leading egypt into chaos. in 2014, the egyptian people legitimized his action by electing him president of the republic. since then, it has been fighting islamist terrorism relentlessly, both ideologically and militarily. he thus boldly affirms the need to renew islam in order to combat the most obscurantist tendencies of this religion. that is why the european union should support marshal al-sissi instead of blaming him for this or that human rights violation, because if his regime were to collapse, it is a country of 92 million inhabitants, egypt, that would risk turning to islamism and lending a hand to terrorism. the tragedy we have just experienced in strasbourg should encourage the european parliament to be more realistic. our mission is to protect europeans, not to lecture our partners.
mr president, the islamist attack in france that took place in strasbourg on tuesday should teach us that in politics we must choose between friends and enemies. it's the identification of the enemy that transforms a politician into a statesman, like winston churchill. marshal al-sissi in egypt understands the danger of islamism and the muslim brotherhood. his speech at al-azhar university in cairo in 2015 was the declaration, before the highest authority of sunni islam, that islamist extremism also finds its roots in an interpretation of islam itself. president al-sissi, a muslim, is currently seeking to have the muslim brotherhood listed as a terrorist organization. the hostile resolutions tabled against egypt by the liberal, socialist and communist groups in this chamber do not explain the context of its difficult action. do you think, ladies and gentlemen, that radical islam respects human rights better? in the face of the camp that has chosen to make war on us, you have chosen, in the words of churchill, dishonor and you will have war, with civil war, also in our country, because islamism is in our country.
mr president, since john magufuli came to power in 2015, the situation in tanzania has been deteriorating, and this has been particularly true since the beginning of the year. journalists, bloggers, political opponents, human rights defenders can be arrested at any time, or even murdered. on 22 february, mr godfrey luena, a member of parliament for the main opposition party, was machete-wielded to death outside his home. six television stations, two radio stations have been suspended. in march, a new communications law made any online radio or tv antenna subject to a license and a 900 euro tax, an exorbitant sum for the country. any content that causes annoyance or leads to public disorder can now be removed via a new law on cybercrime. homosexuality is punishable by 30 years to life in prison, and the dar es salaam regional commissioner has threatened to round up all suspected homosexuals for anal testing and conversion therapy. girls are subjected to sexual violence and forced marriages and are excluded from school if they become pregnant. however, tourism is growing, especially in the beautiful serengeti region. this could be a boon if land controls for speculative purposes did not exacerbate tensions in the region to the detriment, in particular, of the maasai people. it seems that tingatinga, the "bulldozer", as the president is nicknamed, is now destroying much more than it is building.

in writing. rare diseases, which are not so rare, affecting 30 million europeans, remain the poor relative of research. progress is certainly undeniable: the concerted action of europeans, notably through the orphanet database, should be welcomed. private research is also being mobilized more than ever before, not to mention the promise of gene therapy. however, the challenges are considerable: le figaro noted that two thirds of the 30 000 children who come to the institute of genetic diseases have still not been diagnosed. many of them (35%) will die before the age of one, even though the average time to diagnosis is four years. this is a real crossroads for patients and their families, who often have to cope alone with the diagnostic error and, in general, with a considerable emotional and material burden. it is urgent to continue our efforts to promote european research, particularly through programmes such as e-rare, as joint action seems particularly appropriate in this case.
